**CI.** I have understood the meaning quite well and admit that all things harmonize very well. Therefore, it seems time to proceed to the next.

### XV. TANSILO.

Here you see a serpent that languishes in the snow, where a digger had thrown it; and a naked child burning in the midst of fire, with certain other minute details, and the motto that says, IDEM, ITIDEM, NON IDEM <note>original: "The same, in the same way, not the same."</note>. This seems to me more like an enigma than anything else, so I do not presume to explain it completely. However, I would believe that it wishes to signify the same troublesome fate, which torments one and the other in the same way, that is, most intensely and without mercy unto death, with different instruments or contrary principles, showing itself to be the same in cold and in heat. But this seems to me to require a longer and more distinct consideration. **CI.** Another time. Read the rhyme.

829. Since religion resides in the highest parts of a man, and from those highest parts his lower parts live and shine, and because Mahomet <note>original: "Mahumedes"</note> dwells in their minds along with their religion, therefore some Mahomet is always placed in their view. And so that they may turn their faces toward the East, upon which is the Lord, he is placed below the Christian center <note>original: "Meditullium"</note>. It is not the Mahomet himself who wrote the Koran, but another who performs his office; nor is it always the same one, but he is changed. Once it was a man from Saxony who, having been captured by the Algerians, became a Mahometan. Because he had also been a Christian, he was at times moved to speak with them about the Lord, that He was not the son of Joseph, but the Son of God Himself. Others have since succeeded this Mahomet. In the place where that representative Mahomet has his seat, a fire appears like a torch so that he may be recognized; but that fire is not visible to others than Mahometans.

830. The Mahomet himself who wrote the Koran does not come into view today. It was told to me that in earlier times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over all things of their religion as God, he was cast out from his seat, which he had under the Pontificials <note>original: "Pontificiis"</note>—the Catholics—and lowered to the right side near the south. Once, a certain society of Mahometans was stirred up by malicious persons to acknowledge Mahomet as God. To settle this sedition, Mahomet was lifted up from the lower earth and shown, and then he also appeared to me. He appeared similar to those corporeal spirits who have no interior perception, with a face tending toward black, and I heard him speaking these words, *I am your Mahomet*; and he soon seemed to sink down.

831. Mahometans are hostile to Christians primarily because of the belief in three Divine Persons, and consequently the worship of three Gods, as many Creators; and furthermore toward the Roman Catholics because of their genuflections before images. They call the latter idolaters and the former fanatics, saying that they make a three-headed God <note>original: "Deum Tricipitem"</note> and that they say "one" but mutter "three," and thus that they divide Omnipotence, making three out of one and of a single being; and that they are like fauns <note>original: "Fauni"</note> with three horns, one for every god and all together three for one, and that they pray thus, chant thus, and sound off from their pulpits thus.

832. Mahometans, like all nations that acknowledge one God and love justice and do good out of religion, have their own Heaven, but it is outside the Christian one. However, the Mahometan Heaven is divided into two. In the lower one, they live honestly with several wives, but from there no others are raised into the higher Heaven except those who renounce concubines and acknowledge the Lord our Savior, and at the same time His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but it is possible for them to believe that He rules over the Heavens and Hells because He is the Son of God the Father. This faith among them is that through which ascent into the higher Heaven is granted to them by the Lord.

833. That the Mahometan religion has been received by more kingdoms than the Christian religion can be a scandal to those who think about Divine Providence and at the same time believe that no one can be saved unless they are born a Christian. But the Mahometan religion is not a scandal to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence; these inquire where it is, and they also find it. It is in this, that the Mahometan religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the Wisest of all, and also as the Son of God. But because they have made only the Koran the book of their religion, and therefore Mahomet, who wrote it, has settled into their thoughts, and they pursue him with some worship, they therefore think little about our Lord. In order that it may be fully known that this religion was raised up by the Divine Providence of the Lord to abolish the idolatries of many nations, it will be told in some order, but first concerning the origin of idolatries. Before that religion there was the worship of idols

# OBSERVATIONS OF THE STARS

You will encounter a gathering of stars. Furthermore (which is even more marvelous), the stars which have been called "nebulae" by astronomers down to this day are in fact clusters of stars packed together in a wonderful way. From the mingling of their rays, while each individual star escapes the keenness of our eyes due to its small size or its extreme distance from us, that brightness arises which, until now, has been believed to be a denser part of the sky capable of reflecting the rays of the stars or the Sun. We have observed several of these; and we have chosen to append the star charts of two of them.

In the first, you have the nebula called the Head of Orion, in which we have counted twenty-one stars.

The second contains the nebula called the <term>Praesepe</term> <gloss>Manger or Beehive Cluster</gloss>, which is not just one star, but a collection of more than forty little stars: we have noted thirty-six of them, excluding the <term>Aselli</term> <gloss>Little Donkeys</gloss>, arranged in the order that follows.

<note>A telescopic star chart of the Orion Nebula, showing twenty-one individual stars. This historically significant drawing by Galileo Galilei represents one of the first telescopic proofs that nebulae are composed of stars.</note>

->NEBULA OF ORION.<-

There is yet another property <margin>5</margin> specifically that the greater terms have as their difference towards the smaller terms those very smaller terms; and according to these same principles, the difference compared to the difference itself differs by the smaller term when the terms are set out in a <term>duple</term> <gloss>double, or 2 to 1</gloss> ratio. But in a <term>triple</term> <gloss>3 to 1</gloss> ratio, the terms will have a difference twice the value of the term below them, and the differences will likewise be double <margin>10</margin>; in a <term>quadruple</term> <gloss>4 to 1</gloss> ratio, three times; and in a <term>quintuple</term> <gloss>5 to 1</gloss> ratio, four times; and so on infinitely. <margin>4</margin> Not only do geometric proportions occur in multiple ratios, but also in all forms of <term>epimoric</term> <gloss>superparticular, such as 3 to 2</gloss> ratios, <margin>15</margin> <term>epimeric</term> <gloss>superpartient, such as 5 to 3</gloss>, and mixed ratios. The exceptional property of this <term>mediety</term> <gloss>proportional mean</gloss> is preserved in all of them: in continuous proportions, the product of the extremes is equal to the square of the mean; while in disjunct proportions or those with more terms, even if they are not continuous but are of an even number, the product of the extremes is equal to the product of the means. <margin>20</margin> <margin>5</margin> Let this be a sufficient and self-evident example for us that the property of this proportion is preserved in all relations: in every kind of multiple, every kind of epimoric, every kind of epimeric, and every kind of mixed relation; it is that example in which we modeled the proportions starting from equality <note>Nicomachus refers to his previously explained method of generating all ratios from a series of equal terms.</note>.

<summary>Nicomachus describes the unique properties of geometric proportions, specifically how the ratios of differences mirror the ratios of the terms themselves. He also defines the fundamental rule that the product of the extremes equals the square of the mean or the product of the middle terms.</summary>

it often happened that he would flee from those who possessed great skill in dialectic. Regarding his lifestyle, he was not simple, yet within extreme temperance, he made use of expensive things. He took pleasure in white clothing and continued to bathe twice a day in the public baths. Once, when someone asked him why he, being a bishop, bathed twice a day, he replied: Because I cannot manage a third time. At another time, while he was seeing Bishop Sergius, he was asked by one of Arsacius’s followers why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a priest should clothe himself in white. He said: You tell me first where it is written that a bishop must wear black clothing. When the questioner was at a loss, Sisinnius <note>Sisinnius was the Novatian bishop in Constantinople known for his wit and learning</note> followed up on his counter-question: You would not be able to show that a priest must be clothed in black. But Solomon advised me, saying: Let your garments be white <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels appears using white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah wearing white to the apostles. Having said these and many other things readily, he was greatly admired by those present.

When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia <note>specifically Little Galatia</note>, took away a church from the Novatians while he was visiting Constantinople, Sisinnius came to him and requested him to return the church. But Leontius answered warmly and said to him: You Novatians <note>a rigorist Christian sect that refused readmission to those who lapsed during persecution</note> ought not to have churches, for you do away with repentance and shut out the loving-kindness of God. When Leontius said these and many other such harsh things against the Novatians, Sisinnius replied: Indeed, no one has repented as much as I have. When the other asked again: How have you repented? Sisinnius answered: Because I saw you.

Once when John <note>John Chrysostom, the Bishop of Constantinople</note> was accusing him of something and saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said: Indeed it does not. John became angry and said: You see that you alone are a bishop by your own counsel. Sisinnius replied: I do not say that, but that I am not a bishop to you alone, as I am to the ears of others. John, being provoked by what was said, replied: I will stop you from preaching, for you are a heretic. To this, Sisinnius answered gracefully: I will even give you a reward if you release me from such great labor. John, softened by the response, said: I will not stop your freedom of speech if speaking grieves you at all.

Thus Sisinnius was ready with responses and full of grace. To write and record all the things spoken by him would be a long task. Therefore, I have shown through these few examples what kind of man he was to have been chosen to lead. I say this: everyone knows him for his education, and because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Moreover, all the illustrious members of the Senate loved and admired him. Many books were written by him, using a style where he mixes in poetic expressions. He was admired more when speaking than when being read; for such grace was in him—in his face, his voice, his posture, his look, and the whole movement of his body. He was loved for these reasons by all the religions <note>referring to various Christian sects and perhaps non-Christians</note>, and especially by Bishop Atticus. Such are the matters concerning Sisinnius.

Suppose now that a person wishes, by means of a life annuity, to ensure a capital for their heirs, payable at the end of the year of their death. To determine the value of this annuity, one can imagine that the person borrows as a life annuity this capital divided by unity increased by the rate of interest, and places it at perpetual interest at the same fund. It is clear that this capital will be owed by the fund to their heirs at the end of the year of their death; but they will only have paid, each year, the excess of the life interest over the perpetual interest. The table of life annuities therefore shows what the person must pay annually to the fund to ensure this capital after their death.

Maritime insurance, insurance against fire and storms, and generally all establishments of this kind, are calculated by the same principles. A merchant has ships at sea, and wants to insure their value and that of their cargo against the dangers they may encounter. For this, they pay a sum to a company, which guarantees the estimated value of their cargoes and ships. The ratio of this value to the sum that must be given as the price of the insurance depends on the dangers to which the ships are exposed, and can only be assessed by numerous observations on the fate of ships that departed from the port for the same destination.

If the insurer only gave the insurance company the sum indicated by the calculation of probabilities, this company could not cover the expenses of its establishment; the insurer must therefore pay a higher sum as the price of their insurance. But then what is their advantage? It is here that the consideration of moral expectation <note>a concept developed by Daniel Bernoulli, referring to the subjective value or utility of wealth rather than its absolute monetary amount</note> becomes necessary. ## Main Text (Zohar)

Of the radiance—they have all established it. **Rabbi Eleazar** spoke to Isaac: who is the <term>deika katya</term> <gloss>broken spirit</gloss>? Isaac bowed his head. Isaac was <term>deika katya</term> <gloss>broken in spirit</gloss>, he was concerned for his portion; Heaven forbid he should be angry, for his portion was not like the others. And behold, Isaac is from the side of <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Mercy/Kindness</gloss>, yet it is bent? And it is asked: for all of them are <term>Din</term> <gloss>Judgment</gloss>, yet he is from <term>Rachamim</term> <gloss>Compassion</gloss>, and <term>Rachamim</term> <gloss>Compassion</gloss> is the King. Wisdom inherits <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Mercy</gloss>, for <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Mercy</gloss> bows, and Isaac as <term>Din</term> <gloss>Judgment</gloss> is from <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Mercy</gloss>. Isaac bows in <term>Rachamim</term> <gloss>Compassion</gloss>, from which comes harsh <term>Din</term> <gloss>Judgment</gloss>. And thus it was above, this from that, and it emerged from this until that, until all was recognized as one. And all depend on one another, and for all to be found as one, the Heavens are needed forever and ever. **Rabbi Eleazar** recognized that there are no paths for it when we see it as such, and one is desired in both of them to complete everything, such as Jacob, and this is what is written: 
> passing through from end to end <note>Exodus 26:28</note>

The proof is everything, for if you only read from our side and from our side, everything is recognized as being able to rise in one <term>matkala</term> <gloss>balance/scale</gloss>; it does not change or shift, as it is written:
> I am the Lord, I change not <note>Malachi 3:6</note>

**Rabbi Yehuda** said: all of them are radiant cups, depending on one another, and their foundations are as one, all of it, and they are not to be separated. And whoever separates them by his strength is separated from the life of the worlds. **Rabbi Isaac** said: it is written:
> And I will give children to be their princes, and babes shall rule over them <note>Isaiah 3:4</note>

This is what is written regarding the "brazen-faced" <term>Keruvim</term> <gloss>Cherubim</gloss>, and this is what is written, "He who sits upon the Cherubim," and it is written, "And He rode upon a Cherub and did fly." "He who sits upon the Cherubim" refers to when He begins to dwell in assistance; it is written "He who sits upon the Cherubim" <note>this is when He is found in perfection</note>. "And He rode upon a Cherub" <note>singular</note> refers to when the King does not dwell upon His throne. "He who sits upon the Cherubim" <note>plural</note> is two. Woe to the world when one Cherub turns its face away, for it is written:
> and their faces shall look one to another <note>Exodus 25:20</note>

This is when there was peace in the world. **Rabbi Isaac** said: we have learned, "the nakedness of a daughter-in-law and the youth of your father-in-law you shall not uncover." Woe to one who uncovers their nakedness. In this manner it is written of Jacob: "passing through from end to end." And thus the portion of Israel with the Holy One, Blessed be He, is found in their ornaments, in the manner of that which is above, as it is written:
> Israel, in whom I will be glorified <note>Isaiah 49:3</note>

Come and see, **Rabbi Isaac** said: in former days, when one said to his fellow, "Show me one vessel and take money for it." Now a man says to his fellow, "Take money from me and show me another," and there is no one to taste it and no one to incline his portion, except for those few who are gathered and high unto the Holy One, Blessed be He, as it is written:
> And your people shall all be righteous; they shall inherit the land forever, the branch of my planting, the work of my hands, that I may be glorified <note>Isaiah 60:21</note>

Woe that the money is fulfilled and sustained. **Rabbi Isaac** said: Woe, for I see those who are circumcised, all those who are crowned from the higher knots, they search. Woe that it is fulfilled, and all those who depend below, woe. A window opens within us, opening and being renewed and prepared from the smoke to the order that takes pity on them. And as in the Book of Concealment <note>original: Sifra De-Tzniuta</note> it is proven: woe above, woe below, and all of them rise in one balance. Who is the fear of the book? **Rabbi Hezekiah said**: these sections are all in the Great Palace and fill the whole earth. **Rabbi Yehuda** said: all of them are superior in this way. **Rabbi said**: Woe to the one who deviates and bows, and to the one who does not ascend and bow to them in this way.

### The Parable of the Wheat

A parable of a man who dwelt among the fields and did not know the ways of the city dwellers. He sowed wheat and ate the wheat as it was <note>raw kernels</note>. One day he entered the city, and they brought him a good loaf of bread. He said: what is this man eating? They said: it is bread to eat. He ate and found it very tasty. **The Rabbi said**: This is made from greatness. They said: it is wheat. Later they brought him cakes kneaded in oil. He tasted them and said: surely these are exquisite. They said: they are wheat. Later they brought him royal pastries made with honey and oil. He said: and these sweets, how are they made? They said: they are wheat. He said: certainly I am the master of all these things, for I eat the essence of all these, which is wheat. And because of that...

It uses a parable of a rustic man eating raw wheat to illustrate how common people only see the external form of the Torah, while the wise understand the sophisticated "pastries" of its inner mystical meanings.</summary>

For any person who has a portion in the holy people, it is most necessary of all for their faith to receive the <term>Ushpizin</term> <gloss>sacred guests/spiritual visitors</gloss> and to rejoice in this world and in the world to come. A person must make the poor rejoice, for the portion of those guests whom he invites belongs to the poor. > When the clouds gathered, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew away to Lake Manasa. One eighth of the flock flew from the water's edge to a forest of land-growing lotuses. O young girl, three pairs of swans were seen playing with great passion in the water filled with tender lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of swans in that flock. 3

**Word Order and Connection:** O young girl! Upon the arrival of the rainy season, ten times the square root of the swan flock went to Manasa. An eighth part flew from the shore and went to a forest of land-growing lotuses. Three pairs of swans were seen eagerly engaged in play in water adorned with young lotus stalks. Therefore, tell the total number of the flock. 3

**Meaning:** O my dear one, sixteen years of age! There was a flock of swans. When the monsoon arrived, ten times the square root of their number went to Lake Manasa. One-eighth of them flew from the edge of the water into a grove of land-growing lotuses <note>the *sthala-padmini* is a hibiscus variety that resembles a lotus</note>. Three pairs of swans, which equals 6 birds, were seen playing very lovingly in water beautiful with soft lotus fibers. Tell me, how many swans were in that flock? 3

**Mathematical Setup:** The multiplier of the square root <term>mulaguna</term> is 10. The fraction <term>ashtamsha</term> <gloss>1/8</gloss>. The visible remainder <term>drishyam</term> <gloss>6</gloss>. As per the rule stated previously for subtracting or adding fractions, we divide the visible quantity and the square root multiplier by 1 minus the fraction <note>1 minus 1/8 equals 7/8</note>. Dividing by this fraction <gloss>7/8</gloss> results in: Visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>; Multiplier of the root <gloss>80/7</gloss>; Half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss>; The square of this half <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. Adding the visible quantity gives <gloss>1936/49</gloss>. The square root of this is <gloss>44/7</gloss>. Adding half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squaring the result gives the flock of swans: 144.

**Expansion:** Following the rule mentioned in the second verse, we subtract the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> from one. Thus, <gloss>1/1 minus 1/8</gloss> equals <gloss>7/8</gloss>. We divide the visible quantity 6 by this. <gloss>6/1 divided by 7/8</gloss> equals <gloss>6/1 multiplied by 8/7</gloss>, which is <gloss>48/7</gloss>. This becomes our adjusted visible quantity. Similarly, we divide the square root multiplier 10 by the same fraction. <gloss>10/1 divided by 7/8</gloss> equals <gloss>10/1 multiplied by 8/7</gloss>, which is <gloss>80/7</gloss>. This is our adjusted root multiplier. Now, taking <gloss>48/7</gloss> as the visible amount and <gloss>80/7</gloss> as the root multiplier, we perform the operation according to the method in the previous verse. That is, half of the root multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. Squaring this gives <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. This is then added to the visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>...

<margin>Soto, Book 4, Question 7, Article 2. Covarruvias on the chapter "Peccatum" [Sin], Part 2, Section 1. Silvester on the term "Restitutio" [Restitution], number 3, question 6.</margin> These are commonly proposed by theologians who instruct the internal tribunal of the mind.

III. First, it is evident that a possessor in good faith (for a possessor in bad faith is held liable beyond the value of the item due to his own action) is not required to make any restitution if the item has perished, because he neither possesses the item nor has he gained anything from it.

<margin>Medina on Contracts, Question 10.</margin>
IV. Second, a possessor in good faith is required to restore the existing fruits <note>In legal terms, "fruits" refer to the produce or profits generated by an item, such as crops, interest, or rental income.</note> of the item. I specify the fruits of the item, for the fruits of one's own industry—even if they would not have been produced without the item—are not owed to the owner of the item. The cause of this obligation arises from ownership, for he who is the owner of the item is naturally the owner of the fruits of that item.

<margin>Zeffi, Book 2, Chapter 14. Navarrus, Chapter 17, number 7.</margin>
V. Third, a possessor in good faith is held liable for the restitution of both the item and the consumed fruits, provided that he would have consumed just as much in any other way, for in this respect he is considered to have been enriched. Thus, <term>C. Caesar Caligula</term> <gloss>Roman Emperor</gloss> is praised regarding the beginning of his reign for having added the fruits of the intervening time to those to whom he restored kingdoms.

<margin>Suetonius, Chapter 16.</margin>
VI. Fourth, he is not held liable for fruits that he neglected to gather, because he neither has the item nor anything that succeeds in the place of the item.

VII. Fifth, if such a possessor gives an item that was gifted to him to another, he is not held liable unless he would have gifted just as much even without this item, for in that case, the gain consists of having spared his own property.

<margin>Law "Qui vades," final section, Digest of Theft.</margin>
VIII. Sixth, if he sells an item that he purchased, he is not held liable except to the extent that he perhaps sold it for more. But if he sells an item that was gifted to him, he is held liable to restore the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price and would not have otherwise squandered it.

<margin>Law "Si et rem," Digest on the Petition of Inheritance.</margin>
IX. Seventh, an item belonging to another that was purchased in good faith must be returned, and the price expended cannot be recovered. To this rule, it seems to me, an exception must be added: unless the owner could not have reasonably recovered possession of his item without some expenditure, for instance, if the item was in the hands of pirates. In such a case, it may be deducted how much the owner would have willingly spent. For the possession of the deed itself, especially when recovery is difficult, is something of value, and in this, the owner is considered to have been enriched after the loss of the item. And therefore, while the purchase of one's own item is not valid under ordinary law, <term>Paulus Iurisconsultus</term> <gloss>Paul the Jurist</gloss> states that it is valid if it was agreed from the beginning that possession, which is held by another, is to be purchased. Nor do I require here that the item be purchased with the intention of returning it to the owner, a case in which some say an action of <term>negotiorum gestio</term> <gloss>management of affairs</gloss> arises.

# AGAINST CELSUS IV 30. 31.

<note>Celsus</note> says that the Jews were fugitives from Egypt, who never performed any noteworthy deed, nor were they ever held in any account or number. Concerning the fact that they were not fugitives, and that they were not Egyptians but Hebrews who had settled in Egypt, we have already spoken in the preceding sections. <note>Origen refers to Book III, chapters 5—8.</note> If he thinks he can prove they were of no account or number because no history of them is found among the Greeks, we shall say that if anyone were to spend time studying their original constitution and the arrangement of their laws, he would find that they were men who displayed a shadow of a heavenly life upon the earth. <note>Compare Job 8:9 and Hebrews 10:1.</note> Among them, no other was recognized as God except the One over all, and no maker of images was permitted to be a citizen. For neither painter nor sculptor existed in their commonwealth, since the law expelled all such people from it, so that there would be no pretext for the construction of statues. <note>Origen likely draws here from the Jewish philosopher Philo.</note> Such things attract the attention of foolish men and drag the eyes of the soul down from God toward the earth. There was also a law among them to this effect: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved image, any likeness or representation of male or female, the likeness of any beast that is on the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies under heaven, the likeness of any creeping thing that creeps on the earth, the likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters under the earth." <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 4:16—18.</note> And the law intended that by dwelling on the truth regarding each thing, they should not create other things contrary to the truth—falsifying the truly male or the truly female, or the nature of beasts, or the race of birds, or of creeping things, or of fish.

The following is also solemn and magnificent among them: "Lest, looking up to heaven and seeing the sun and the moon and the stars, the whole host of heaven, you be led astray and worship them and serve them." <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 4:19.</note>

What a constitution it was for an entire nation, among whom it was not even possible for an effeminate man to appear! <note>Referring to the prohibitions in Deuteronomy 23:1 and 17.</note> It is also wonderful that the fuels of youthful passion, the prostitutes, were removed from their commonwealth. <note>Referring to Deuteronomy 23:17.</note> There were also courts consisting of the most just men, who had given ample proof of a healthy life. <note>Referring to Exodus 18:21 and Deuteronomy 1:15.</note>

<summary>Origen defends the Jewish nation against Celsus's claims of insignificance by highlighting the moral and spiritual superiority of the Mosaic Law, specifically its strict prohibition of idolatry and immorality.</summary>

<margin>Commentary by Su <note>Su Che, 1039 to 1112, a prominent Song dynasty scholar</note></margin> One who does not know the Way but applies themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily, yet they have no means to unify it. This inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: To hear much and select what is good to follow, or to see much and remember it, is only the second level of knowledge. If one day you know the Way, you will look back at falsehoods. Every false action is a delusion. To discard delusion and return to one's true nature is called "decrease." Confucius said to Zigong: Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all? Zigong replied: Yes, is it not so? Confucius said: No, I permeate everything with a single thread. Forgetting the mind to purely return to nature is what we call decrease. Once delusions no longer exist, and one has even forgotten the act of forgetting, the mind returns to nature entirely. Then one can act without departing from <term>wu wei</term> <gloss>non-action or effortless action</gloss>. All people have the desire to take hold of the world and manage its affairs. Because they create activities and seek results, their intentions are visible externally, and things resist them. Therefore, success is difficult to achieve. The Sage practices non-action and thus has no ulterior motives in his heart. When his heart is visible externally, all things are at peace with him. Though he does not strive to take the world or manage its affairs, the affairs of the world naturally follow and find peace.

<margin>Commentary by Lü <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032 to 1111, a high official and scholar of the Song dynasty</note></margin> Practicing learning is for those who have not yet heard the Way. Since they have not heard it, they must seek it broadly; thus it is said that learning "increases." Practicing the Way is for those who have already heard the Way. Having heard it, they must practice it through non-action; thus it is said that the Way "decreases." To decrease and further decrease means one has not yet escaped the realm of "doing." Only when one even decreases the act of decreasing does one reach the state of non-action. Non-action means being still and unmoving. "Doing nothing is left undone" means that when stimulated, one penetrates all the causes under heaven. Moving from "doing" to "non-doing" is what is called the constant. Learning without worry is called divine. The direction of the divine is the Way. Who can attain this level of divinity? From this we see that to take the world, one must always use non-action. If one uses "doing," it is clear they are not fit to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai <note>A Southern Song dynasty scholar</note></margin> Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires daily increase. Only after being able to do anything can one speak of the Way; therefore, the Way desires daily decrease. However, increase can be sought through progress, while decrease is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly shed their attachments and reach the land of non-action. Thus they can do anything, and their applications are inexhaustible, spreading across the world with ample room.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai <note>Likely the Daoist scholar Li Daichun, Yuan dynasty</note></margin> Practicing learning is the means to seek knowledge, so it increases daily. Practicing the Way is the means to remove delusion, so it decreases daily. If knowledge is not perfected, then decrease cannot be complete; thus daily increase provides the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then there is non-action. Upon reaching non-action, then all that is "done" has never not been "non-doing." This state cannot be easily discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When non-action reaches its peak, though the things of the world are many, a single thread permeates them. If one uses "business" to create more "business," it is difficult to find leisure. Even a single object can become entangled and chaotic, how much more so the vastness of the world?

The Sage has no fixed heart <note>or mind</note>; he takes the heart of the people as his own heart. Those who are good, I treat as good. Those who are not good, I also treat as good; thus virtue is goodness. Those who are faithful, I trust. Those who are not faithful, I also trust; thus virtue is trust. The Sage dwells in the world with a cautious and clouded mind, making the heart of the world simple and whole. The people all focus their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage <note>The text breaks here and continues on the next page.</note>

A pure maiden, untouched, for the deities below,
Drawn by lot from the blood of the <term>Aepytidae</term> <gloss>descendants of Aepytus</gloss>,
Sacrifice her in nocturnal slaughter.
But if she fails the slaughter, or is from another, then
Let another be offered, giving himself to the slaughter willingly.

When the god had revealed these things, they immediately cast lots for all the maidens who were of the family of the <term>Aepytidae</term>. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. However, Epebolus the seer forbade her sacrifice, claiming she was not truly the daughter of Lyciscus; he asserted that Lyciscus's wife, being unable to bear children, had secretly substituted the girl as her own. While Epebolus was explaining this matter, Lyciscus took the maiden and fled to Sparta. The Messenians were disheartened when they realized Lyciscus had escaped, but then Aristodemus, a man of the <term>Aepytidae</term> lineage and more distinguished than Lyciscus in general reputation and military matters, offered his own daughter to be sacrificed of her own will.

Human ambition is often hidden by fate, just as a pebble is covered by the silt of a river. At that moment, as Aristodemus strove to save the Messenians, the following obstacle arose. A certain Messenian man (whose name they do not mention) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus and was soon to take her as his wife. At first, he entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, claiming that because she was betrothed to him, Aristodemus was no longer the master of the girl, and that he, as the betrothed, had more authority over her. When he saw this was not succeeding, he turned to a shameful argument: he claimed he had slept with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. Finally, he drove Aristodemus to such a point that, maddened by rage, the father killed his daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and demonstrated that she was not with child.

Epebolus, who was present, then ordered that someone else must offer a daughter; he claimed that the death of Aristodemus’s daughter achieved nothing for them, as her father had murdered her rather than sacrificing her to the gods as the <term>Pythia</term> <gloss>the priestess of Apollo at Delphi</gloss> had commanded. When the seer said this, the Messenian multitude rushed to kill the girl’s suitor, believing he had brought a useless pollution upon Aristodemus and made their hope of salvation uncertain. However, this man was a very close friend to Euphaes. Euphaes persuaded the Messenians that the oracle was fulfilled by the death of the girl and that what Aristodemus had done was sufficient for them. When he said this, all those of the <term>Aepytidae</term> family agreed, for their own fear for their daughters ceased. Everyone complied with the kings' advice and dissolved the assembly, turning instead to sacrifices and a festival for the gods.

The Lacedaemonians <gloss>Spartans</gloss>, hearing of the oracle given to the Messenians, were also disheartened, as were their kings, and they hesitated to begin a battle. In the sixth year after Lyciscus fled from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians, finding the omens favorable, marched against Ithome. The Cretans were no longer present with them, and the Messenians' allies also arrived late. The Spartans were already viewed with suspicion by other Peloponnesians, especially the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives intended to arrive secretly to assist against the Lacedaemonians, acting more out of private initiative than a common decree. The Arcadians had openly forbidden the expedition, yet they did not arrive either. The fame of the oracle led the Messenians to risk battle even without allies. For the most part, nothing different happened than in the previous battle; the daylight failed while they were still fighting. It is not recorded that either wing or any company was forced back, for they say they did not keep the ranks they had at the start. Instead, the best men from both sides met in the center, and there the whole struggle took place. Euphaes, showing more daring than was expected of a king, recklessly pressed upon the troops around Theopompus, receiving many wounds, some of which were incurable. Fainting from loss of blood...

Any portion of the Torah <note>the Five Books of Moses</note> that mentions the name <term>YHVH Elohim</term> refers to actions performed through the combined attributes of the Attribute of Justice <note>Hebrew: Middat ha-Din</note> and the Attribute of Mercy <note>Hebrew: Middat ha-Rachamim</note>. You will find this regarding the creation of the first man, his judgment, his expulsion from Eden, and all those matters. You will find they were all executed through both Justice and Mercy, in perfect completeness, with Justice according to what was strictly true and Mercy according to what was appropriate.

Following this principle, the Torah states: The Rock, His work is perfect <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>. The explanation of the verse is this: The Rock, who decrees judgment with strength, does not act with cruelty. He does not decree judgment until His work is "perfect," meaning that the decree was first deliberated by both attributes, Loving-kindness <note>Hebrew: Chesed</note> and Justice. This is the meaning of "His work is perfect" <term>tamim</term>.

The term <term>tamim</term> <gloss>perfect/complete</gloss> is a secret referring to two things together. It is as if one said <term>te'omim</term> <gloss>twins</gloss>, but the language of honor uses the term <term>tamim</term> for these two supernal matters, while for earthly things it uses the term <term>te'omim</term>. Thus it says, and they shall be doubled <term>te'omim</term> from below, and they shall be complete <term>tamim</term> together at the top <note>Exodus 26:24</note>. Below they are "twins" because they appear as two separate things, opposites like an advocate and an accuser. But above, all is a single intention. Between the advocate and the accuser, both share one purpose. There is no hatred or love there, and no partiality, only true judgment. Therefore it says "His work is perfect," meaning He consulted Justice and Mercy and then decreed the judgment. This is the secret of "True Judgment."

Regarding the phrase, for all His ways are justice <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>, it means this is evident to every observer. You already know that <term>Mishpat</term> <gloss>Justice/Judgment</gloss> is comprised of both Justice and Mercy. <term>Mishpat</term> corresponds to Jacob, who is the Middle Pillar, balancing between the two "tents" of Abraham and Isaac. Abraham corresponds to Loving-kindness, Isaac corresponds to Justice, and Jacob decides between them: a plain man <term>ish tam</term>, dwelling in tents <note>Genesis 25:27</note>. <term>Mishpat</term> corresponds to Jacob, drawing from the Loving-kindness of Abraham's side and the Justice of Isaac's side. Thus it says, You have executed justice <term>mishpat</term> and righteousness <term>tzedakah</term> in Jacob <note>Psalm 99:4</note>.

The Prophet said: O Lord <term>YHVH</term>, correct me, but with justice <term>mishpat</term>; not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing <note>Jeremiah 10:24</note>. The explanation is: "Correct me, Lord, but with justice," where the word "but" <term>ach</term> implies a partition—meaning, through the half of the attribute of Justice that is Mercy. Since <term>Mishpat</term> is half Justice and half Mercy, he says "but with justice" and follows with "not in Your anger," revealing the secret of diminishing the half of Justice that stems from "Anger."

Therefore, <term>Mishpat</term> depends on Jacob, who is the "Father of the Tribes." Having known the great pain of children, when the Holy One decrees upon them, Jacob seeks mercy and righteousness for them. The secret is: And the Lord of Hosts shall be exalted in justice <note>Isaiah 5:16</note>. What is written immediately after? And God the Holy One is sanctified in righteousness. This means when the Judgment is collected, the Justice rests and turns toward the attribute of <term>El</term> <gloss>God</gloss>. This is the secret of "And God the Holy One is sanctified in righteousness." Whenever the name <term>YHVH Tzevaot</term> is exalted in justice, the attribute of <term>El</term>, which is higher, arrives and performs righteousness, and Justice is served. This is the secret of the saying that <term>Mishpat</term> is included in Loving-kindness and Justice.

There is a great secret in the verse: Righteousness <term>Tzedek</term> and Justice <term>Mishpat</term> are the foundation of Your throne <note>Psalm 89:15</note>. Sometimes <term>Tzedek</term> <gloss>Righteousness</gloss> acts as strict Justice depending on how the flow is received, for <term>Tzedek</term> can be a harsh judgment in its strength. However, when <term>Mishpat</term> is partnered with it, the Throne is established with Mercy. And if it is exalted through <term>Mishpat</term> and reaches the point where Loving-kindness and Truth meet, they are called "The Shining Face." Then everything becomes great Mercy, and this is the secret of "shall go before

The essence and refinement of it is the distribution of Justice and Kindness according to the recipients who are prepared for them through spiritual awakening. In the Zohar <note>Parashat Balak</note> it is discussed how the Ancient of Ancients <term>Atika de-Atikin</term> is entirely white <note>pure mercy</note>. When everything is unified, everything becomes life. Everything is balanced before the paths separate to the right and left. From our side, Justice appears, but the secret of Justice is surrendered to the Holy Head. It is written, "The voice of the Lord is upon the waters." This means all His ways are <term>Mishpat</term>. <term>Mishpat</term> is a revealed way, visible to all below, whereas supernal matters may be hidden. Thus it is written regarding Job, that he spoke without knowledge. The explanation is that the secret was revealed to him only in part, as the sages said. The attribute of Justice is gathered under the hand of Loving-kindness, included within it as a foundation.

# TO THE HIGH AND NOBLE LORD,

In the months of April and May of the year 1716, an abundance of haddock was brought into our city, which came to us from the seaside villages of Katwyk, Schevelinge, and Ter-Hey; many of which were still alive, which we call <term>Krimp-fchelvis</term> <gloss>a term for haddock that is still quivering or fresh enough to shrink when touched or prepared</gloss>, and on some days they were so cheap that they were bought for less than a stuiver <note>a small Dutch coin</note> apiece. And such has also occurred some years ago.

Reflecting upon the multitude of these very tasty haddock, which were being caught with nets at that time, whereas they are otherwise caught with bait placed upon a fishhook, I imagined that there must be a reason why the small haddock approached our sea coasts in such abundance, seeing as a month or two later, not a single haddock was caught on our coasts.

I imagined that the abundance of the small haddock was dependent upon the bait, or food, that they were finding on our sea coasts.

And the angel answered and said to me: "These are the four spirits of heaven, going forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth. The one with the black horses goes forth to the north country, and the white ones go forth after them, and the spotted ones go forth to the south country." And the strong ones went forth and sought to go, to walk to and fro through the earth; and he said: "Go, walk to and fro through the earth." So they walked to and fro through the earth. Then he cried out to me and spoke to me, saying: "Behold, those who go toward the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country."

**And he answered.** These are the four spirits. Like "to the four spirits." And similarly, "and he came to Jerusalem" is like "into Jerusalem." Another interpretation: "to the son of a black man" is like "the black son." And things similar to it. This refers to the division of the four chariots, which go out to the four directions of the heavens. This is to give permission to the four kingdoms to rule in the four directions, each one in its time. This refers to the whole world, which is a place of strength. **From standing before the Lord of all the earth.** That is, on a mission from God who gave them power over this. As it says: "And the sons of God came to stand before the Lord." <margin>Job 2</margin>

**The one with.** The black ones. He mentions the black ones because the time of the kingdom of Babylon had already passed. The kingdoms of Media and Persia went first to the north country, for they were there to destroy it, and afterward they ruled over all the kingdoms of the earth. **And the white ones**, which are the kingdom of Greece, went out after them once the kingdom was established. For Alexander of Macedon, the first king of Greece, killed Darius in Babylon and took the kingdom from him and reigned, and afterward his successors ruled throughout the whole world.

**And the spotted ones go forth to the south country.** This refers to the Roman portion, because Rome is <term>shannunit</term> <gloss>perhaps "swallow-like" or "changing"</gloss>. Augustus Caesar, who ruled over Rome, began to fight against the kingdom of Greece. At the start of his wars, he went out to the land of Egypt, which is in the south. In those days, the sons of Greece ruled all the lands. Then Augustus Caesar overpowered them, transferred the kingdom from the sons of Greece, and returned it to the Romans.

**And the strong ones.** These are a hint to the kingdom of Ishmael <note>A common medieval Jewish reference to the Islamic Caliphates</note>, who strengthened themselves of their own accord to seek a kingdom, to find a place that would be for them a spirit. This is what is meant by: "And they sought to go, to walk to and fro through the earth." **And he said.** Meaning, He gave them permission to travel and conquer lands. **Then he cried out.** Meaning, He called to me with a great voice and said to me: **"Behold, those who go toward the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country."** This refers to the portion of the black horses who went out to Babylon to destroy it.

4. Laziness and lack of effort are obstacles to wealth. Lack of grooming and lack of adornment are obstacles to physical appearance. Unwholesome behavior is an obstacle to health. Then <term>Manjushri</term> <gloss>the Bodhisattva of Wisdom</gloss>, the Ever-Youthful, spoke thus to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, it is difficult, truly very difficult, for these <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>beings dedicated to enlightenment</gloss> <term>Mahasattvas</term> <gloss>great beings</gloss> to endure this out of reverence for the Blessed One. How, O Blessed One, should this <term>Dharma-paryaya</term> <gloss>Discourse of the Great Law</gloss> be proclaimed by these Bodhisattva Mahasattvas in the latter age, in the latter time?"

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to Manjushri, the Ever-Youthful: "A Bodhisattva Mahasattva who is established in four qualities, Manjushri, should proclaim this Discourse of the Great Law in the latter age, in the latter time. What are these four? Here, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva who is established in proper conduct and proper spheres of association should proclaim this Discourse of the Great Law in the latter age, in the latter time. And how, Manjushri, does a Bodhisattva Mahasattva become established in proper conduct and proper spheres of association?

When, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva is patient, self-controlled, has reached the level of the disciplined, whose mind is neither terrified nor startled, and who is not envious; and when, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not practice within the field of any particular phenomena <note>original: "dharma"</note>, but views the true nature <note>original: "yatha-bhutam"</note> of all things according to their own characteristics. That which involves no fixation and no conceptualization regarding these things—this, Manjushri, is called the proper conduct of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva.

And what, Manjushri, is the proper sphere of association of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva?
<margin>K 276</margin>
W 236
When a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not serve a king, nor serve, associate with, attend upon, or approach princes, high ministers, or royal officials. He does not serve, associate with, or attend upon followers of other schools, such as wandering mendicants <note>original: "caraka-parivrajaka"</note>, the <term>Ajivikas</term> <gloss>a fatalist sect</gloss>, or the <term>Nirgranthas</term> <gloss>the Jains</gloss>, nor those beings devoted to worldly poetry and treatises. He does not serve, associate with, or attend upon those who hold to the spells of the materialists <note>original: "lokayata"</note>, nor those who follow materialism, nor does he become intimate with them.

He does not associate with <term>Chandalas</term> <gloss>outcastes</gloss>, boxers, swine-breeders, poultry-keepers, deer-hunters, butchers, actors, dancers, or wrestlers. He does not frequent other places of amusement or play belonging to others, nor does he become intimate with them. Only when such people have approached him does he preach the Law to them from time to time, and he preaches it without attachment.

<margin>N 181</margin>
Furthermore, he does not serve, associate with, or attend upon monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who belong to the <term>Sravaka-yana</term> <gloss>the Disciple Vehicle/Hinayana</gloss>, nor does he become intimate with them. He does not share the same sphere of movement with them, whether in a walking path or in a monastery. Only when they have approached him does he preach the Law to them from time to time, and he preaches it without attachment. This, Manjushri, is the proper sphere of association of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva.
<margin>K 277</margin>

Furthermore, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not preach the Law frequently to women by seizing upon the signs of attraction for one reason or another, nor does he constantly desire the sight of women. He does not enter the homes of families, nor does he think he must frequently converse with young girls, maidens, or daughters-in-law, nor does he exchange greetings with them. He does not preach the Law to eunuchs, nor does he become intimate with them or exchange greetings with them. He does not enter a house alone for the sake of alms, unless he is practicing the <term>Tathagatanusmriti</term> <gloss>mindfulness of the Buddha</gloss>. Then <term>Manjushri</term> <gloss>the Bodhisattva of Wisdom</gloss>, the Ever-Youthful, spoke thus to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, it is difficult, truly very difficult, for these <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>beings dedicated to enlightenment</gloss> <term>Mahasattvas</term> <gloss>great beings</gloss> to endure this out of reverence for the Blessed One. How, O Blessed One, should this <term>Dharma-paryaya</term> <gloss>Discourse of the Great Law</gloss> be proclaimed by these Bodhisattva Mahasattvas in the latter age, in the latter time?"

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to Manjushri, the Ever-Youthful: "A Bodhisattva Mahasattva who is established in four qualities, Manjushri, should proclaim this Discourse of the Great Law in the latter age, in the latter time. What are these four? Here, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva who is established in proper conduct and proper spheres of association should proclaim this Discourse of the Great Law in the latter age, in the latter time. And how, Manjushri, does a Bodhisattva Mahasattva become established in proper conduct and proper spheres of association?

When, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva is patient, self-controlled, has reached the level of the disciplined, whose mind is neither terrified nor startled, and who is not envious; and when, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not practice within the field of any particular phenomena <note>original: "dharma"</note>, but views the true nature <note>original: "yatha-bhutam"</note> of all things according to their own characteristics. That which involves no fixation and no conceptualization regarding these things—this, Manjushri, is called the proper conduct of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva.

And what, Manjushri, is the proper sphere of association of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva?
<margin>K 276
W 236</margin>
When a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not serve a king, nor serve, associate with, attend upon, or approach princes, high ministers, or royal officials. He does not serve, associate with, or attend upon followers of other schools, such as wandering mendicants <note>original: "caraka-parivrajaka"</note>, the <term>Ajivikas</term> <gloss>a fatalist sect</gloss>, or the <term>Nirgranthas</term> <gloss>the Jains</gloss>, nor those beings devoted to worldly poetry and treatises. He does not serve, associate with, or attend upon those who hold to the spells of the materialists <note>original: "lokayata"</note>, nor those who follow materialism, nor does he become intimate with them.

He does not associate with <term>Chandalas</term> <gloss>outcastes</gloss>, boxers, swine-breeders, poultry-keepers, deer-hunters, butchers, actors, dancers, or wrestlers. He does not frequent other places of amusement or play belonging to others, nor does he become intimate with them. Only when such people have approached him does he preach the Law to them from time to time, and he preaches it without attachment.

<margin>N 181</margin>
Furthermore, he does not serve, associate with, or attend upon monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who belong to the <term>Sravaka-yana</term> <gloss>the Disciple Vehicle/Hinayana</gloss>, nor does he become intimate with them. He does not share the same sphere of movement with them, whether in a walking path or in a monastery. Only when they have approached him does he preach the Law to them from time to time, and he preaches it without attachment. This, Manjushri, is the proper sphere of association of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva.
<margin>K 277</margin>

Furthermore, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not preach the Law frequently to women by seizing upon the signs of attraction for one reason or another, nor does he constantly desire the sight of women. He does not enter the homes of families, nor does he think he must frequently converse with young girls, maidens, or daughters-in-law, nor does he exchange greetings with them. He does not preach the Law to eunuchs, nor does he become intimate with them or exchange greetings with them. He does not enter a house alone for the sake of alms, unless he is practicing the <term>Tathagatanusmriti</term> <gloss>mindfulness of the Buddha</gloss>. Even if he preaches the Law to women, he does not preach it with any passion for the Law, much less...

However, certain superstitious people and children of this age, wishing to heap errors upon errors beyond the intellect and intention of <term>Scotus</term> <gloss>John Duns Scotus, a medieval theologian</gloss> and the canonists, attempt to defend themselves with these arguments. They claim that natural things possess certain hidden virtues for which no reason can be assigned by man, just as the magnet attracts iron, and many other things which <term>Augustine</term> <gloss>Saint Augustine of Hippo</gloss> enumerates in book twenty-one of *The City of God*. Therefore, they argue, in matters of seeking health where medicinal and natural remedies fail, it should not be illicit if one seeks to procure health for oneself or another through things such as non-necromantic and astrological images, or through rings and similar objects. 

Likewise, they argue: just as natural bodies are subject to celestial bodies, so too do artificial bodies, such as images, acquire certain hidden virtues following the influence of celestial bodies. Therefore, artificial bodies, such as images, also acquire some hidden virtues from celestial bodies to cause certain effects, and thus to use them and others of this kind is not illicit. Furthermore, demons can transmute bodies in many ways, as <term>Augustine</term> states in book three of *On the Trinity*, and this is evident in those who are bewitched. Therefore, they argue, it is licit to use their power to remove those afflictions. 

But in truth, the statements of all holy doctors are to the contrary, as has been shown here and there. Therefore, to the first point, it is said that if natural things are used simply to produce effects for which they are thought to have a natural virtue, it is not illicit. If, however, they add characters or any other unknown and vain observations which manifestly do not have a natural efficacy, this will be superstitious and illicit, as <term>Thomas</term> <gloss>Thomas Aquinas</gloss> treats in the *Summa Theologica*, part two of the second part, question ninety-six, article two, at the end of the question.

<summary>This text addresses the arguments used by superstitious individuals to justify the use of magical objects, such as talismans and amulets, for healing by claiming they operate through natural or celestial influences; the author refutes these claims by referencing established theological authority.</summary>
<keywords>superstition, natural virtues, celestial influence, artificial images, demonic influence, Saint Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, illicit practices</keywords>

<margin>They use the heart and the tongue for the inundation of Egypt.</margin>
A sacred water-vessel <note>original: "Θεία δ’ ὑδρεία"</note> signifies either the sky and the earth gushing forth water, or the vessel itself, which they liken to a heart that possesses a tongue. It is compared to a heart because among the Egyptians, this organ is the ruling part of the body <note>original: "τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν"</note>, just as the Nile is established as the ruler of Egypt. It is likened to a tongue because the tongue always exists in moisture and they call it the generator of that which is good. Two water-vessels <note>original: "βία δὲ ὑδρεῖα"</note> signify neither more nor less <note>the balanced state of the river</note>, because the process of the inundation is twofold according to them. They designate one vessel for the land of Egypt, because Egypt is capable of generating water by itself. The other vessel is designated for the Ocean, for from the Ocean water comes into Egypt at the time of the rising of the river. They also attribute the rising to the rains that occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia during the season of the Nile’s inundation. That Egypt itself generates water can be understood from this fact: in the rest of the world's climates, the flooding of rivers is completed during the winter.

<summary>This page explains the hieroglyphic use of water-vessels to represent the Nile's inundation, comparing the river's vital role in Egypt to the heart's role in the body. It describes the Egyptian belief that the flood stems from both local sources and the external Ocean or Ethiopian rains.</summary>
<keywords>Nile inundation, water-vessel, heart, tongue, Egypt, Ethiopia, hydrology, symbolism</keywords>

The Moon is the companion and follower of the Sun. Its names are also many. Among them is <term>Soma</term> <gloss>fortunate</gloss> because it is a lucky star; lucky stars are called <term>subha-graha</term> <gloss>fortunate planets</gloss> and unlucky ones are called <term>papa-graha</term> <gloss>evil planets</gloss>. Other names include <term>Nishisha</term> <gloss>Lord of the Night</gloss>, <term>Nakshatranatha</term> <gloss>Lord of the Lunar Mansions</gloss>, <term>Dvijeshvara</term> <gloss>Lord of the Twice-born</gloss>, and <term>Shitanshu</term> <gloss>Cold-rayed</gloss>. This is because its sphere is watery and contains moisture. When the Sun's rays fall upon it, they cool down due to its inherent coldness. The rays then reflect, illuminating the darkness, cooling the night, and extinguishing the burning damage caused by the Sun. For this reason, it is also called <term>Chandra</term> <gloss>the Shining</gloss>. It is the left eye of <term>Narayana</term> <gloss>the Supreme Deity</gloss>, just as the Sun is his right eye. Let Your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let Your pious ones sing for joy. For the sake of David Your servant, do not turn away the face of Your anointed. <term>Lamnatzeach</term> <gloss>For the conductor</gloss>, a Psalm of David: May the Lord answer you in the day of distress; may the name of the God of Jacob set you on high. May He send your help from the sanctuary and support you from Zion. May He remember all your offerings and accept your burnt sacrifices. <term>Selah</term> <gloss>forever</gloss>. May He grant you according to your heart and fulfill all your counsel. We will sing for joy in Your salvation, and in the name of our God we will wave our banners; may the Lord fulfill all your requests. Now I know that the Lord saves His anointed; He answers him from His holy heavens with the saving might of His right hand. Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will mention the name of the Lord our God. They have bowed down and fallen, but we have risen and stand upright. O Lord, save! May the King answer us on the day we call. And a redeemer shall come to Zion and to those who turn from transgression in Jacob, says the Lord. And as for Me, this is My covenant with them, says the Lord: My spirit which is upon you, and My words which I have placed in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your children, nor from the mouth of your children's children, says the Lord, from now and forever.

And You are holy, enthroned upon the praises of Israel. And one called to another and said: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts, the whole earth is full of His glory. <note>The following is the Aramaic Targum translation of the previous verse, traditionally recited in the 'Uva Le-Tziyon' prayer.</note> And they receive word from one another and say: Holy in the highest heavens, the house of His Presence; Holy upon the earth, the work of His power; Holy forever and for all eternity. The Lord of Hosts, the whole earth is full of the radiance of His glory. Then a spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the voice of a great rushing: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place. <note>Aramaic translation follows:</note> And a spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me a voice of great movement of those who praise and say: Blessed is the glory of the Lord from the place of the house of His Presence. The Lord shall reign forever and ever. The Lord, His kingdom stands forever and ever. O Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, keep this forever as the inclination of the thoughts of the hearts of Your people, and direct their hearts toward You. And He, being merciful, forgives iniquity and does not destroy; frequently He turns away His anger and does not stir up all His wrath. For You, Lord, are good and forgiving, and abundant in kindness to all who call upon You. Your righteousness is an everlasting righteousness, and Your Torah is truth. You will give truth to Jacob and kindness to Abraham, as You have sworn to our fathers from days of old. Blessed be the Lord day by day; He carries us, the God of our salvation. <term>Selah</term>. The Lord of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our stronghold. <term>Selah</term>. O Lord of Hosts, happy is the man who trusts in You. O Lord, save! May the King answer us on the day we call. Blessed is He, our God, who created us for His glory and separated us from those who go astray, and gave us a Torah of truth and planted eternal life within us. May He open our heart through His Torah and place in our heart love and awe of Him, to do His will and to serve Him with a perfect heart, so that we do not labor in vain nor give birth for terror. May it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our fathers, that we keep Your statutes in this world, and merit to live and see and inherit goodness and blessing in the years of the Messianic age and for the life of the World to Come. So that my glory may sing to You and not be silent; O Lord my God, I will thank You forever. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his trust. Trust in the Lord forever, for in God the Lord is an everlasting Rock. And those who know Your name will trust in You, for You have not forsaken those who seek You, O Lord. The Lord desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to magnify the Torah and make it glorious.

<column-break/>

O Lord, our Master, how majestic is Your name in all the earth.
Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who hope in the Lord.

And now, may the power of the Lord be great, as You have spoken, saying: Remember Your mercies, O Lord, and Your kindnesses, for they are from of old.

<note>This begins the Mourner's Kaddish prayer in Aramaic.</note>
Magnified and sanctified be His great name in the world which He created according to His will. May He establish His kingdom and cause His salvation to sprout and bring near <note>alternative reading: the end/arrival of</note> His Messiah. In your lifetime and in your days and in the lifetime of the whole House of Israel, speedily and in a near time; and say, Amen. May His great name be blessed forever and to all eternity. Blessed and praised, glorified and exalted, extolled and honored, adored and lauded be the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, above <note>from time to time, and above all</note> all blessings and songs, praises and consolations that are uttered in the world; and say, Amen. Receive, receive with mercy and favor our prayer. May the prayers and supplications of the whole House of Israel be accepted before their Father who is in heaven; and say, Amen. Receive: May the name of the Lord be blessed from now and forever.

May there be abundant peace from heaven, and life upon us and upon all Israel; and say, Amen. My help is from the Lord, Maker of heaven and earth. He who makes peace in His high places, may He make peace upon us and upon all Israel; and say, Amen.

A prayer of David: Incline Your ear, O Lord, answer me, for I am poor and needy. Guard my soul, for I am pious; save Your servant who trusts in You, You are my God. Be gracious to me, O Lord, for I call to You all day long. Gladden the soul of Your servant, for to You, O Lord, I lift up my soul. For You, Lord, are good and forgiving, and abundant in kindness to all who call upon You. Give ear, O Lord, to my prayer, and listen to the voice of my supplications. In the day of my distress I call to You, for You will answer me. There is none like You among the gods, O Lord, and there are no works like Yours. All nations whom You have made shall come and bow down before You, O Lord, and shall honor Your name. For You are great and perform wonders; You alone are God. Teach me, O Lord, Your way, I will walk in Your truth; unite my heart to fear Your name. I will thank You, O Lord my God, with all my heart, and I will honor Your name forever. For Your kindness is great toward me, and You have rescued my soul from the lowest depths. O God, the arrogant have risen against me, and a company of violent men have sought my soul; they have not set You before them. But You, Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abundant in kindness and truth. Turn to me and be gracious to me; give Your strength to Your servant, and save the son of Your handmaid. Work for me a sign for good, that those who hate me may see it and be ashamed, for You, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me.

House of Jacob, come and let us walk in the light of the Lord. For all the peoples walk each in the name of its god, but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God forever and ever.
May the Lord our God be with us as He was with our fathers; may He not leave us nor forsake us. To incline our hearts to Him, to walk in all His ways and to keep His commandments, His statutes, and His ordinances which He commanded our fathers. And may these words of mine, with which I have made supplication before the Lord, be near to the Lord our God day and night, that He may maintain the cause of His servant and the cause of His people Israel, as each day requires. So that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord is God; there is no other.

A song of ascents, by David: If the Lord had not been for us—let Israel now say—If the Lord had not been for us when man rose up against us, then they would have swallowed us alive in the heat of their anger against us. Then the waters would have overwhelmed us, the stream would have passed over our soul. Then the treacherous waters would have passed over our soul. Blessed be the Lord, who has not given us as prey to their teeth. Our soul escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare broke, and we escaped. Our help is in the name of the Lord, Maker of heaven and earth.

Suspicious means she has developed doubts about the suitor. Guarded means she is protected by strong attendants. Fearful refers to her fear of her husband. Under her mother-in-law means she is under the direct supervision of her husband's mother. He should not pursue her, meaning he should not desire her, knowing his own limitations. ### Chapter 3

Even when advances are made, women who are steady and bold must be tested. Such women do not reveal their true feelings easily, and therefore special efforts are required. For this reason, the examination of intentions is now discussed:

A man making advances should observe the behavior of the woman; by doing so, her true intentions are tested. 1.

Just as one approaches a maiden, he should observe her behavior, meaning her physical gestures and actions. By observing these, her internal state or intention is tested. 1.

How she is to be won is stated:

If she does not reveal the secret, he should win her over through a female messenger. 2.

Does not reveal the secret means she does not openly show her sexual feelings. Because of her boldness, he should win her over using a female messenger. 2.

If she rejects an advance but continues to associate with him, he should know her mind is divided; he should win her over gradually. 3.

After she has rejected the advance made by the hero <note>original: "nayaka"</note>, if she stays away for a few days and then once again associates with him or seeks his company, he should recognize her as having a divided mind. Because she is a subject for testing, she feels "I do not know what I should do." He should win her over by degrees and not abandon her suddenly. 3.

A specific detail regarding this is mentioned:

If she rejects an advance but then appears again specifically well-adorned, then likewise...

Now, after Xiangling had met everyone and finished her evening meal, and while Baochai and the others went to Lady Wang's quarters, she made her way to the Bamboo Lodge <note>original: "Xiaoxiang Guan", the residence of Lin Daiyu</note>. By this time, Daiyu was mostly recovered. Seeing that Xiangling had come to live in the garden, she was naturally pleased. Xiangling said with a smile, "Now that I have moved in and have some free time, if you would only teach me how to compose poetry, it would be my great good fortune!" 

Daiyu laughed and replied, "Since you wish to learn poetry, you must take me as your master. Although I am not truly proficient, I know enough to teach you the basics." 

Xiangling smiled and said, "If that is truly so, I shall take you as my master. You must not grow weary of me."

Daiyu said, "What difficulty is there in it that it should be so hard to learn? It is nothing more than the <term>Qi-Cheng-Zhuan-He</term> <gloss>Introduction, Elucidation, Transition, and Conclusion</gloss>. The middle sections, the elucidation and transition, consist of two sets of couplets: level tones against deflected tones, empty words against solid words, and solid against empty. If you truly have a remarkable line, you can even ignore the rules of tonal balance and formal structure."

Xiangling laughed, "No wonder I often peek at one or two poems in old books and find some that are perfectly balanced while others are not. I have also heard it said that 'the first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Yet in the poems of the ancients, some follow this and others are wrong on the second, fourth, or sixth syllables. I have been puzzled every day. Now that I hear you speak, it seems these rules do not matter much after all, as long as the phrasing is novel and original."

Daiyu said, "That is exactly the point. Phrasing is, after all, a secondary matter; the most important thing is the intent. If the intent and the mood are genuine, the poem will be good even without polished phrasing. This is called 'not letting the words damage the meaning.'"

Xiangling said, "I simply love Lu Fangweng's <note>the poet Lu You</note> lines: 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, keeping the fragrance long; the old inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It is so vivid and interesting!"

Daiyu replied, "Because you do not yet understand poetry, you like what is shallow and accessible. Once you fall into that pattern, you will never be able to escape it. Listen to me: if you truly wish to learn, I have here the <term>Wang Mojie Quanji</term> <gloss>The Collected Works of Wang Wei</gloss>. Take his one hundred five-character regulated poems and study them until you have thoroughly mastered them. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>referring to Du Fu</note> seven-character regulated poems. Next, read one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>referring to Li Bai</note> seven-character quatrains. With the work of these three as your foundation, you can then look at the works of Tao Yuanming, Ying Yang, Liu Zhen, Xie Lingyun, Ruan Ji, Yu Xin, and Bao Zhao. Since you are such an exceptionally clever and bright person, in less than a year’s time, you need not worry about not becoming a true poet!" 

Hearing this, Xiangling smiled and said, "In that case, dear Miss, please bring that book out for me. I will take it back and read a few poems at night." 

Upon hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijuan to bring Wang Wei's five-character regulated poems and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Only look at those marked with red circles; those are the ones I have selected. Read them one by one. If there is anything you do not understand, ask your mistress <note>Baochai</note>, or if you run into me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the Alpinia Park <note>original: "Hengwu Yuan", Baochai’s residence</note>. Ignoring all other affairs, she began to read them one by one under the lamp. Baochai urged her several times to go to sleep, but she would not. Seeing her such devotion, Baochai had no choice but to let her be.

One day, just as Daiyu had finished washing and dressing, Xiangling arrived with a beaming face to return the book and ask for the poems of Du Fu. 

Daiyu asked with a smile, "How many do you remember?" 

Xiangling smiled and said, "I have read all of those marked with red circles." 

Daiyu asked, "Have you gained any insight from them?" 

Xiangling laughed, "I have indeed gained some insight, though I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell you what I think."
