> At the arrival of the clouds <note>the monsoon season</note>, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew toward Lake Manasa. One eighth of the flock flew from the water’s edge toward a forest of land-growing lotuses. Oh young girl, three pairs of swans were seen sporting lovingly in the water, which was beautiful with young lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of swans in that flock. 3

**Word-by-word connection:** Oh girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of the swan flock went to Lake Manasa. One eighth part flew from the shore of the water and reached a land-lotus forest. And three pairs of swans were seen engaged in play in the water adorned with young lotus roots. Therefore, tell the total number of the flock. 3

**Meaning:** Oh beloved, who is sixteen years of age! There was a flock of swans. From that flock, when the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root <note>of the total population</note> went away to Lake Manasa. One eighth part of the flock flew from the water's edge into a forest of land-lotuses. Three pairs of swans <note>totaling six birds</note> were seen playing with great affection in water made beautiful by tender lotus stalks. Say then, how many swans were in that flock? 3

**Statement of the problem:** Square root multiplier: 10; eighth part: <gloss>1/8</gloss>; visible amount: <gloss>6</gloss>. As it was stated <note>in the previous rule</note> that the quantity is decreased by the fractions, here the visible amount and the square root multiplier are divided by one minus the fraction <gloss>7/8</gloss>. The resulting visible amount is <gloss>48/7</gloss> and the square root multiplier is <gloss>80/7</gloss>. Half of this multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. Its square <gloss>1600/49</gloss> added to the product of the visible amount results in <gloss>1936/49</gloss>. The square root of this is <gloss>44/7</gloss>. Added to half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and then squared, the total flock of swans is found: 144.

**Elaboration:** According to the rule mentioned in the second verse, the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> was subtracted from one <note>the whole</note>, thus <gloss>1/1 - 1/8</gloss> = <gloss>7/8</gloss>. The visible quantity of 6 was divided by this, so <gloss>6/1 ÷ 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>6/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>48/7</gloss>. In this way, after performing the conversion by seven, <gloss>48/7</gloss> became the visible quantity <term>drishya rashi</term> <gloss>the known constant in the equation</gloss>. Similarly, the square root multiplier of 10 was divided by <gloss>7/8</gloss>, which is <gloss>10/1 ÷ 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>10/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>80/7</gloss>. After the conversion by seven, <gloss>80/7</gloss> became the root-multiplier quantity. Now, taking <gloss>48/7</gloss> as the visible quantity and <gloss>80/7</gloss> as the square root multiplier, the calculation was performed according to the method mentioned in the previous verse. That is: half of the root multiplier became <gloss>40/7</gloss>. This was squared to become <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. This was then added to the visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>...

ON THE LAW OF WAR

<margin>Sotol. IV. q. 7. art. 2. Covar. ad c. peccatum. par. II. §. I. Silv. in verbo Restitut. n. 3. quæ. 6.</margin>
These matters are commonly proposed by theologians who instruct the internal tribunal of the conscience <note>original: "internum animi tribunal"</note>.

III. First, it appears that a possessor in good faith (for a possessor in bad faith is held liable for more than the value of the thing, due to his own action) is not held liable for any restitution if the thing has perished: because neither is the thing itself with him, nor has he gained anything from the thing.

<margin>Medina de contr. q. 10. Zeff. l. II. c. 14. Navar. c. 17. n. 7.</margin>
IV. Second, a possessor in good faith is held liable for the restitution of even the existing fruits <gloss>income or produce</gloss> of the thing: I say the fruits of the thing; for the fruits of industry, even if they would not have proceeded without the thing, are not owed to the owner of the thing. The cause of this obligation arises from ownership. For he who is the owner of a thing is naturally also the owner of the fruits of that thing.

V. Third, a possessor in good faith is held liable for the restitution of both the thing and the consumed fruits, provided that he would have consumed just as much in any other way: for in this regard, he is considered to have become wealthier. Thus, <note>the Roman Emperor</note> Gaius Caesar Caligula is praised in the accounts of his early reign, for when he restored kingdoms to those from whom they were taken, he added the fruits accrued during the interim period.

<margin>Suet. c. 16.</margin>
VI. Fourth, he is not held liable for the fruits which he neglected to gather: because he neither has the thing, nor anything that succeeds in the place of the thing.

VII. Fifth, if such a possessor gives to another a thing that was given to him, he is not held liable unless he would have donated just as much even without this thing: for in that case, the gain would be the preservation of his own property.

<margin>L. Quivæs. §. ult. D. furti.</margin>
VIII. Sixth, if he sells a thing he bought, he is not held liable, unless perhaps he sold it for more: but if he sells a thing that was given to him, he is held liable for the restitution of the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price, which he otherwise would not have squandered.

<margin>L. fi & rem. D. de petit. hereditatis. L. Sed & fi lege. D. eod. L. Si eum servum. D. de rebus creditis.</margin>
IX. Seventh, a thing belonging to another, bought in good faith, must be returned, and the price paid cannot be reclaimed. To this rule, it seems to me that this exception should be added: unless the owner could not reasonably have recovered possession of his property without some expense, for example, if the thing was in the hands of pirates. In such a case, it may be deducted how much the owner would have willingly spent. For the possession of the fact itself, especially when recovery is difficult, is something of value, and in this, the owner is considered to have been made wealthier after the loss of the thing.

<margin>L. Mater tua. L. Si mancipia. D. de rei vindicatione. L. Sucr. D. de cont. emt. L. 1. D. de evictionibus.</margin>
And therefore, although the purchase of one's own property is not valid under ordinary law, the jurist Paulus states it is valid if it was agreed from the beginning that the possession which is in the hands of another should be purchased. Nor do I require here that the thing be purchased with the intent that it be returned to the owner; for in that case, there are those who say that an action for the management of affairs <note>original: "negotiorum actionem"</note> arises.

<margin>L. Si laborav. §. Si navis. D. ad legem Rhodiam. pern. v. quid de prædam ementibus. Ægid. Reg. diff. 35. dub. 7. num. 126. Hoft. tit. de a L. Si in emtione §. rei. D. de contr. emt.</margin>

# AGAINST CELSUS IV. 30. 31.

<note>Celsus</note> says that the Jews were fugitives from Egypt who never achieved anything of importance, nor were they ever held in any account or numbered among significant peoples. Regarding the claim that they were not fugitives, and that they were not Egyptians but Hebrews who had settled as sojourners in Egypt, we have already spoken in the preceding sections. <note>original: "Vgl. oben III 5—8." Reference to Origen's earlier defense of the Jewish exodus.</note>

But if Celsus thinks he can establish that they were never of any account or number based on the fact that the Greeks do not find much history concerning them, we shall reply as follows. If anyone were to examine their original constitution and the arrangement of their laws, he would find that they were men who displayed a shadow of the heavenly life upon the earth. <note>A reference to the Platonic and Pauline idea that earthly forms are shadows of heavenly realities.</note> Among them, no other God was recognized except the One over all, and no maker of images was permitted to be a citizen. For neither painter nor sculptor existed in their commonwealth, since the law expelled all such persons from it, so that there might be no pretext for the construction of images. Such things attract the attention of foolish men and drag the eyes of the soul down from God toward the earth.

Indeed, there was a law among them to this effect: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved image, any likeness of a form, whether male or female, the likeness of any beast that is on the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies under heaven, the likeness of any creeping thing that creeps on the earth, the likeness of any fish that is in the waters beneath the earth." <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 4:16—18.</note> For the law intended that they, by communing with the truth concerning each thing, should not fashion other things contrary to the truth, which would give a false representation of the truly male, or the truly female, or the nature of beasts, or the genus of birds, or of creeping things, or of fish.

Also solemn and magnificent among them is the command: "Lest you look up to heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, the entire host of heaven, and be led astray to worship them and serve them." <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 4:19.</note>

What a constitution it was for an entire nation, among whom it was not even possible for an <term>thelydria</term> <gloss>effeminate man/catamite</gloss> to be seen! It is also wonderful that the incitements of the young, namely harlots, were removed from their commonwealth. There were also courts of justice composed of the most righteous men, who had long given proof of a healthy life.

<summary>Origen defends the historical dignity of the Jews against Celsus by highlighting the moral and spiritual superiority of the Mosaic Law, specifically its prohibition of idolatry and its promotion of a heavenly way of life.</summary>

<meta>This page contains commentary on Chapters 48 and 49 of the Tao Te Ching. The layout consists of four distinct commentaries by Su, Lü, Huang Maocai, and Xizhai, followed by the main text of Chapter 49.</meta>

<margin>Su's Commentary <note>Su Zhe, 1039 to 1112, a prominent Song dynasty official and scholar.</note></margin> One who does not know the Way <term>Dao</term> but devotes themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily. However, without a single principle to unify this knowledge, it inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: Hear much and select what is good to follow; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge. If one day you know the Way, you will look back at falsehoods. Every false action is a delusion. To remove delusion and return to one's true nature is called "decreasing." Confucius asked Zigong: Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all? He replied: Yes, is it not so? Confucius said: No, I pervade everything with a single principle. To forget the mind in order to restore nature purely is what is meant by "decreasing." If delusions still remain, one must continue until both are forgotten. When the mind is purified and nature is restored without remnant, one abandons forced action <term>wei</term> and attains non-action <term>wu wei</term>. All people have the desire to take hold of the world and manage its affairs. Therefore, when they create trouble and seek results, their intentions are visible externally, and things resist them; thus they find it difficult to achieve their goals. The Sage practices non-action and therefore has no concerns in his heart. His inner state is visible externally, and things are at peace with him. Though he does not strive to take the world or manage its affairs, the affairs of the world naturally follow and find peace.

<margin>Lü's Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032 to 1111, a key figure in the New Policies of the Song dynasty.</note></margin> Those who practice learning are those who have not yet heard the Way. Since they have not heard the Way, they must seek it broadly; therefore, it is said that they "increase." Those who practice the Way are those who have already heard it. Having heard it, they must practice it by doing nothing other than non-action; therefore, it is said that they "decrease." To decrease and further decrease means one has not yet avoided having some action. One must even decrease the act of decreasing itself. Only then does one reach non-action. Non-action refers to being silent and unmoving. "Doing nothing left undone" refers to being moved and then penetrating all the causes under heaven. Reaching non-action through the process of non-action is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called divine. The direction of the divine is what is called the Way. Who can attain such supreme divinity? From this we can see that taking the world is always done through non-action. When one relies on forced action, it is clear they are insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai's Commentary <note>A Southern Song dynasty scholar known for his works on the Laozi.</note></margin> Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires daily increase. Only after reaching a state where nothing is forced can one speak of the Way; therefore, the Way desires daily decrease. However, increase can be sought through progress, while decrease is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only those of supreme clarity can suddenly cast off burdens and reach the realm of non-action. Thus they can leave nothing undone, and their practical application is inexhaustible. When applied to the world, they act with ample freedom.

<margin>Xizhai's Commentary <note>The art name of Wang Tingzhen, a Yuan dynasty scholar.</note></margin> One practices learning to seek knowledge, thus it increases daily. One practices the Way to remove delusion, thus it decreases daily. If knowledge is not perfected, then the decrease will not be complete. Therefore, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then one reaches non-action. Upon reaching non-action, even when there is action, it has never not been non-action. This state cannot be easily discussed in terms of decrease or increase. When non-action reaches its peak, though the world is vast, it is unified by a single principle. If one creates trouble through busy-ness, then even a single object in front of them remains entangled and chaotic, let alone the vastness of the world.

The Sage has no fixed heart; he takes the heart of the people as his own heart. To those who are good, I am good. To those who are not good, I am also good; thus virtue is goodness. To those who are trustworthy, I trust them. To those who are not trustworthy, I also trust them; thus virtue is trust. The Sage is in the world, blending his heart with the world to make it whole. The people all focus their ears and eyes upon him. The Sage <note>The text cuts off here and continues on the next page.</note>

<page-num>Twenty-two</page-num>

# PAUSANIAS

A maiden pure and untouched by the lower gods,
Chosen by lot from the blood of the <term>Aepytidae</term> <gloss>the royal descendants of Aepytus</gloss>,
You must sacrifice in the nocturnal slaughters.
But if she is withheld from the slaughter, or belongs to another, then
Sacrifice one who is given over to the slaughter willingly.

When the god <note>the Delphic Oracle</note> revealed these things, they immediately cast lots for all the maidens who were of the lineage of the <term>Aepytidae</term>. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. But Epebolus the seer forbade her sacrifice, claiming she was not truly the daughter of Lyciscus; he said that the woman who lived with Lyciscus, being unable to bear children, had secretly substituted the child as her own. While he was explaining these matters concerning her, Lyciscus took the girl and deserted to Sparta. 

The Messenians were disheartened when they realized Lyciscus had fled, but then Aristodemus, a man of the <term>Aepytidae</term> race and of greater renown than Lyciscus in other respects and especially in war, offered his own daughter to be sacrificed willingly. However, fate often conceals human enthusiasm in such matters, just as mud in a river might cover a pebble. Thus, when Aristodemus was striving to save the Messenians, the following obstacle arose. A certain Messenian man (whose name they do not mention) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus. At that time, he was already about to take her as his wife. At first, he entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, arguing that since Aristodemus had betrothed her to him, he was no longer the master of the girl, and that he himself, as her betrothed, had greater authority over her. 

Secondly, when he saw that this was not succeeding, he turned to a shameful argument, claiming that he had been intimate with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. In the end, he drove Aristodemus to such a point that, maddened by rage, he killed his own daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and proved that she was not with child. Epebolus the seer, who was present, then ordered that someone else must give up a daughter; for he said that Aristodemus’s daughter, having died, profited them nothing, as her father had murdered her and had not sacrificed her to the gods as the <term>Pythia</term> <gloss>the priestess of Apollo at Delphi</gloss> had commanded. 

When the seer said these things, the multitude of Messenians rushed to kill the girl’s suitor, as he had brought a needless stain of blood upon Aristodemus and had made the hope of their salvation uncertain. The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, hearing of the oracle given to the Messenians, were also disheartened, and their kings were hesitant to begin a battle. In the months of April and May of the year 1716, an abundance of haddock was brought to our city, which came to us from the seaside villages of Katwijk, Scheveningen, and Ter Heij. Reflecting on the multitude of these very tasty haddock, which were caught at that time with nets, whereas they are otherwise caught with bait placed on a fishing hook, I imagined that there must be a reason why the small haddock approached our sea coasts in such abundance, since a month or two later, not a single haddock was caught on our coasts.

And the angel answered and said to me: "These are the four spirits of the heavens, going forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth. Then he cried out to me and spoke to me, saying: "Behold, those who go toward the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country."

**And he answered.** "These are the four spirits." This is like saying "to the four spirits." Similarly, "and he came Jerusalem" means "to Jerusalem." Another explanation: "to the son of a black man" means "to a black son," and similar cases. This refers to the division of the four chariots going out to the four directions <margin>2 Samuel 10</margin> of the heavens. This means giving authority to the four kingdoms to rule in the four directions, each one in its own time. This refers to the whole world, which is a place of strength. "From standing before the Lord of all the earth" means they act as messengers of God who gave them dominion over this, similar to the verse: "The sons of God came to stand before the Lord." <margin>Job 2</margin>

**The one with.** The black horses. He did not mention the first chariot <note>red horses representing Babylon</note> because the era of the Babylonian kingdom had already passed. The kingdom of Media and Persia went out first to the north country, for they were there to destroy it and afterward ruled over all the kingdoms of the earth.

And the white horses, which are the kingdom of Greece, went out after them once that kingdom was established. For Alexander of Macedon <note>Alexander the Great</note>, the first king of Greece, killed Darius in Babylon and took the kingdom from him and ruled; and afterward his successors ruled throughout the entire world.

**And the dappled ones went forth to the south country.** This refers to the Roman Empire. Because Rome is in the north, and Augustus Caesar <note>transliterated here as Yoichum/Octavius</note>, who ruled over Rome, began to fight the kingdom of Greece. In the beginning of his wars, he went out to the land of Egypt, which is in the south. At that time, the Greeks were ruling in all lands, but Augustus Caesar overcame them, transferred the kingdom from the Greeks, and restored it to the Romans.

**And the strong ones.** These are an allusion to the kingdom of Ishmael <note>the Islamic Caliphate</note> who exerted themselves on their own to seek a kingdom and a place to dwell. This is why it says, "they sought to go, to walk to and fro through the earth."

**And he said.** This means He gave them permission to travel and conquer lands.

**Then he cried out.** That is, he called to me with a loud voice and said to me: **"Behold, those who go toward the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country."** This refers to the portion of the black horses <note>the Persians</note> who went out to Babylon to destroy it.

The dialogue highlights the contrast between traditional religious adherence and the Buddha's path of letting go.</summary>

->Chapter 13: The Chapter on Peaceful Practices<-

<margin>K 275</margin>
N 180
W 235
Then <term>Manjushri</term> <gloss>the Bodhisattva of Wisdom</gloss>, the Ever-Youthful, spoke to the Blessed One: Lord, it is difficult, extremely difficult, what these <term>bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>beings seeking awakening</gloss> and <term>mahasattvas</term> <gloss>great beings</gloss> have undertaken out of reverence for the Blessed One. Lord, how should this <term>dharmaparyaya</term> <gloss>exposition of the Law/Lotus Sutra</gloss> be proclaimed by these bodhisattvas and mahasattvas in the later times, in the final age? 

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke to Manjushri, the Ever-Youthful: Manjushri, when established in four principles, a bodhisattva and mahasattva should proclaim this exposition of the Law in the later times, in the final age. Which four? Here, Manjushri, a bodhisattva and mahasattva who is established in proper conduct <note>original: "acara"</note> and proper sphere of association <note>original: "gocara"</note> should proclaim this exposition of the Law in the later times, in the final age. 

And how, Manjushri, is a bodhisattva and mahasattva established in proper conduct and proper sphere of association? When a bodhisattva and mahasattva is patient, self-controlled, has reached the level of the disciplined, is not terrified or anxious in mind, and is not envious. And when, Manjushri, a bodhisattva and mahasattva does not dwell upon any phenomena <note>original: "dharma"</note> but observes the true nature of things as they are. That which is the non-clinging and non-conceptualization regarding these phenomena is called the proper conduct of a bodhisattva and mahasattva.

And what, Manjushri, is the proper sphere of association for a bodhisattva and mahasattva? 
<margin>K 276</margin>
W 236
When a bodhisattva and mahasattva does not frequent kings, nor does he frequent princes, royal ministers, or royal officers. He does not associate with, serve, or approach them. He does not associate with, serve, or approach followers of other paths <note>original: "anyatirthya"</note> such as wandering mendicants, itinerant monks, members of the <term>Ajivika</term> <gloss>a fatalist sect</gloss> or <term>Nirgrantha</term> <gloss>Jain</gloss> sects, nor those devoted to worldly poetry and secular treatises. He does not associate with, serve, or approach those who maintain worldly or materialistic spells <note>original: "lokayata-mantradharakan"</note>, nor does he form friendships with them. He does not associate with <term>Chandalas</term> <gloss>outcastes</gloss>, those who strike with fists, pig-breeders, poultry-breeders, 
<margin>N 181</margin>
deer-hunters, butchers, actors, dancers, or wrestlers. He does not frequent other places of amusement or play belonging to others. He does not form friendships with them. However, when such people come to him, he preaches the Law to them at the appropriate time, but he does so without relying on them <note>original: "anishrita", meaning without expectation of reward or social attachment</note>. 

He does not associate with, serve, or approach monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who follow the vehicle of the Disciples <note>original: "Shravakayana"</note>, nor does he form friendships with them. He does not frequent the same places with them, whether in walking paths or in monasteries. However, when they come to him, he preaches the Law at the appropriate time, and he does so without relying on them. This, Manjushri, is the proper sphere of association for a bodhisattva and mahasattva.
<margin>K 277</margin>

Furthermore, Manjushri, a bodhisattva and mahasattva does not preach the Law repeatedly to women by seizing upon signs of affection for one or another, nor is he desirous of seeing women repeatedly. He does not frequent the households of others, nor does he think he should converse frequently with girls, maidens, or daughters-in-law, nor does he exchange greetings with them. He does not preach the Law to eunuchs, nor does he form friendships or exchange greetings with them. He does not enter a house alone for the sake of alms, except when he is practicing the mindfulness of the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>the Buddha/Thus-Gone One</gloss>. If he does preach the Law to women, he does not preach even the Law with a mind of attachment to the Law <note>let alone with worldly desire</note>.

<summary>The Buddha explains the first of four "Peaceful Practices" for bodhisattvas in the final age, focusing on proper conduct and avoiding distracting or harmful social associations. The passage details specific groups, such as worldly officials, other religious sects, and certain professions, that a practitioner should avoid to maintain spiritual focus.</summary>
<keywords>Manjushri, Peaceful Practices, Bodhisattva, Proper Conduct, Final Age, Lotus Sutra, Tathagatanusmriti</keywords>

However, certain superstitious people and sons of this age, wishing to accumulate errors upon errors, attempt to defend themselves beyond the understanding and intention of <term>Scotus</term> <gloss>John Duns Scotus, a medieval scholastic philosopher</gloss> and the canonists with these arguments: because natural things have certain hidden virtues whose reason cannot be assigned by man, just as the magnet attracts iron. And many other things which <term>Augustine</term> enumerates in the twenty-first book of *The City of God*. Therefore, they argue, in matters of health, where exorcisms and natural medicines fail, it would not be illicit if one were to seek a cure in oneself or in another through images that are not necromantic or astrological, or through rings and things of this sort.

Likewise, they argue: Just as natural bodies are subject to celestial bodies, so too do artificial bodies, such as images, acquire certain hidden virtues following the influence of celestial bodies. Therefore, artificial bodies, such as images, also acquire some hidden virtues from celestial bodies to cause certain effects; therefore, to use them and others of this kind is not illicit. Furthermore, demons can multiply and transmute bodies, as <term>Augustine</term> says in the third book of *On the Trinity*, and this is evident in those who are bewitched <note>original: "maleficiatis"</note>. Therefore, it is permitted to use even their power to remove those evils.

But in truth, the statements of all holy doctors are to the contrary, as has been shown here and there. Hence, to the first argument, one says that if natural things are simply applied to produce some effect for which they are thought to have a natural virtue, it is not illicit. But if they add characters or any other unknown and vain observations which manifestly do not possess such efficacy by nature, it will be superstitious and illicit, as <term>Thomas</term> <gloss>Thomas Aquinas</gloss> treats in the second part of the second part of the <term>Summa</term> <gloss>Summa Theologica</gloss>, question 96, article 2, at the end of the question.

<summary>This passage addresses and refutes arguments used by superstitious individuals who attempt to justify the use of magical images, rings, and demonic influence for healing by misinterpreting scholastic philosophy and the writings of Saint Augustine.</summary>
<keywords>superstition, natural virtue, Scholasticism, Saint Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, necromancy, celestial influence, illicit practices</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: at the beginning of winter by an excess of moisture.</meta>

<margin>With the fullness... the same... in the middle they use... a heart and a tongue... Egyptian...</margin>
They represent a divine water jar, or the heaven and earth gushing forth water, by likening the water jar to a heart that possesses a tongue. They use the heart because, among the Egyptians, it is the ruling part <note>original: "hegemonikon"</note> of the body, just as the Nile is established as the ruler of Egypt. They use the tongue because it always exists in moisture and they call it the mother of that which is good. There are two water jars, neither more nor less, because the process of the inundation <note>the annual flooding of the Nile</note> is twofold according to them. They designate one as coming from the land of Egypt, since Egypt is itself a generator of water. They designate the other as coming from the Ocean, for water arrives in Egypt from it at the time of the inundation. There is also the grain <note>referring to the harvest</note> caused by the rains which occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia during the season of the Nile's rising. That Egypt itself generates the water can be understood from this: in the rest of the world's climate, the flooding of rivers is completed during the winter.

<summary>This page explains the symbolic use of the water jar, heart, and tongue to represent the Nile's inundation and the unique Egyptian belief that the land itself generates its seasonal floods.</summary>
<keywords>Nile, Egypt, water jar, heart, tongue, inundation, Ethiopia, climate, floods, symbolism</keywords>

of the response. It seems right to me that we should look toward this with wisdom <note>original: φροσύνῃ</note> and honor it. And there are responses given out of love for humanity and with temperance <note>original: σωφροσύνῃ</note>. Concerning those who see their equals and those who are not left behind, even those of the same nature as themselves, who are equally matched and of like passions; for it is not just the middle ground that brings punishment. That which has been spoken as one flows through; and a mind with a lightened burden of the man rejoices. And how could one be loved in anger? On the one hand, I desire what is together; but on the other hand, they also lay waste. Being long and blunt, I do not accept this legislation. I do not accept the agreement. These legislators were men. This is clear from understanding

<column-break/>

the legislation. Consider how much power they give to fathers over their female servants. But the weaker part belongs to human beings. Why should it not be so? But why do they rather press the day? Or how could the present situation exist? This is not according to the Scripture. You are treated violently. And for days they are reckoned. Often indeed it is brought to an end. Likewise, even the good is half-finished. And that which is not of God is not made firm. And a blessing toward the root, such as the work is. And those things which are easy do not take root, they are not meant to last. You see the laws of that legislation: how a man belongs to a woman. Both practice it. The village is mine. Often in such a way, at the same time with the arrangement. Likewise, a man belongs to a woman according to the writings, though for a time there is lawlessness <note>original: παρανομίς</note>.

<summary>Gregory of Nazianzus critiques earthly laws regarding marriage and gender, arguing that human legislation is biased because it was written by men. He contrasts these human standards with the spiritual equality and divine order found in Scripture.</summary>
<keywords>Gregory Nazianzen, legislation, marriage, gender equality, ethics, law, Greek patristics</keywords>

that he began to speak. 12 And the priest of the angel of God <note>referring to the priest of Zeus/Jupiter</note> who was outside the city brought an ox and a crown to the entrance of the house where they were staying, and he wanted to offer a sacrifice to them. 13 When Barnabas and Paul heard this, they tore their clothes and jumped and went out to the place of the multitude and were crying out. 14 And they said, "Men, why are you doing this? We also are human beings like you, with the same feelings as you. We think that you should turn away from these vain things and turn toward the living God. He is the one who made the heavens and the earth, the seas, and everything that is in them. 15 In previous generations, He allowed all the nations to walk in the way of their own choosing. 16 Even so, He did not leave His essence without witness; He did good things for them from the heavens and brought down rain for them, and grew fruits for them in their seasons, and filled them with food and joy in their hearts." 17 And when they had said this, the people saw it and said that no man should offer a sacrifice to them. 18 And Jews came there from Iconium <term>Koniya</term> and from Antioch, and they incited the people against them and stoned Paul. 19 And they threw him outside the city because they thought that he was dead. 20 But the disciples gathered around him, and he stood up and entered the city. On the second day, he and Barnabas went out from there and came to the city of Derbe. 21 And when they had taught the people of that city and many disciples were added to them, they returned to the city of Lystra, to Iconium, and to the city of Antioch. 22 And they strengthened themselves in the faith.

Its companion and successor also has many names. Among them is <term>Soma</term> <gloss>the Moon</gloss> because it is auspicious, and auspicious things are called <term>Saumya-graha</term> <gloss>beneficent planets</gloss>, while the inauspicious are called <term>Papa-graha</term> <gloss>malefic planets</gloss>. Other names include <term>Nishisha</term> <gloss>Lord of the Night</gloss>, <term>Nakshatra-natha</term> <gloss>Lord of the Lunar Mansions</gloss>, <term>Dvijeshvara</term> <gloss>Lord of the Twice-born</gloss>, and <term>Shitanshu</term> <gloss>Cold-rayed</gloss>. This is because its sphere is composed of water, and therein lies its refreshing quality. When the sun's rays fall upon it, they become cold like its own nature and reflect, illuminating the darkness, cooling the night, and extinguishing the burning damage caused by the sun. For this reason, it is also called <term>Chandra</term> <gloss>the Shining</gloss>. It is the left eye of <term>Narayana</term> <gloss>Vishnu</gloss>, just as the sun is his right eye. # Morning Prayer

<note>A decorative printer's ornament is placed here.</note>

On their side, regarding his return to the Dweller <note>God</note>, it is written: For they shall see eye to eye when the Lord returns to Zion. And it is said: And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken. May the Father of Mercy have compassion on the people who have been borne by Him <note>Israel</note>, and remember the covenant of the patriarchs <term>Etanim</term> <gloss>the enduring ones</gloss>, and deliver our souls from evil hours, and rebuke the evil inclination in those who are carried by Him, and graciously grant us everlasting deliverance. May He fulfill our requests in good measure with salvation and mercy.

<note>Decorative ornament</note>

The seat of the Prophets, the book of the fear of the shores, etc. <note>Instructions for returning the Torah scroll to the ark</note>
And this is the Torah which Moses set before the children of Israel, according to the word of the Lord by the hand of Moses.

Praise the name of the Lord, for His name alone is exalted.
His glory is above the earth and heaven; He has lifted up a horn for His people, a praise for all His pious ones, for the children of Israel, the people close to Him, Hallelujah.

And he says in the name of standing for the generation, and it is written... <note>Fragmented liturgical instructions</note>

And with confidence he said: Return, O Lord, to the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel. Arise, O Lord, to Your resting place, You and the Ark of Your strength. Let Your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let Your pious ones sing for joy. For the sake of David Your servant, do not turn away the face of Your anointed. For I have given you good instruction; do not forsake my Torah. It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it, and those who support it are happy. Its ways are ways of pleasantness, and all its paths are peace. Turn us back to You, O Lord, and we shall return; renew our days as of old. Happy are they, etc.

To the Chief Musician, a Psalm of David: May the Lord answer you in the day of distress; may the name of the God of Jacob set you on high. May He send your help from the sanctuary and support you from Zion. May He remember all your offerings and accept your burnt sacrifice, Selah. May He grant you according to your heart and fulfill all your counsel. We will sing for joy in your salvation, and in the name of our God we will set up our banners; may the Lord fulfill all your petitions. Now I know that the Lord saves His anointed; He will answer him from His holy heaven with the saving strength of His right hand. Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will mention the name of the Lord our God. They have bowed down and fallen, but we have risen and stand upright. O Lord, save! May the King answer us on the day we call. And a redeemer shall come to Zion and to those in Jacob who turn from transgression, says the Lord. And as for Me, this is My covenant with them, says the Lord: My spirit which is upon you, and My words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your children, nor from the mouth of your children's children, says the Lord, from henceforth and forever.

But You are holy, O You who dwell amid the praises of Israel. And one called to another and said: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory. <note>The following is the Aramaic translation of the previous verse</note> And they receive sanction from one another and say: Holy in the highest heavens, the house of His Presence; holy upon the earth, the work of His power; holy forever and to all eternity is the Lord of Hosts, the whole earth is full of the radiance of His glory. Then a wind lifted me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great rushing: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place. Then a wind lifted me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great rushing of those who utter praises and say: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from the place of the house of His Presence. The Lord shall reign forever and ever. The Lord, His kingdom stands forever and to all eternity. O Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel our fathers, keep this forever as the inward thought of the heart of Your people, and direct their heart to You. And He, being merciful, forgives iniquity and does not destroy; frequently He turns His anger away and does not stir up all His wrath. For You, Lord, are good and forgiving, and abounding in kindness to all who call upon You. Your righteousness is an everlasting righteousness, and Your Torah is truth. You will show truth to Jacob and kindness to Abraham, as You have sworn to our fathers from the days of old. Blessed be the Lord, day by day He bears our burden, the God who is our salvation, Selah. The Lord of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our stronghold, Selah. O Lord of Hosts, happy is the man who trusts in You. O Lord, save! May the King answer us on the day we call. Blessed be our God who created us for His glory, and separated us from those who go astray, and gave us a Torah of truth, and planted eternal life within us. May He open our heart to His Torah, and place His love and fear in our heart, to do His will and to serve Him with a perfect heart, so that we do not labor in vain nor give birth to terror. May it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our ancestors, that we keep Your statutes in this world, and merit to live and see and inherit the goodness and blessing of the years of the Messianic age and the life of the world to come. So that my soul may sing praise to You and not be silent; O Lord my God, I will give thanks to You forever. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and whose trust the Lord is. Trust in the Lord forever and ever, for in God the Lord is an everlasting Rock. And those who know Your name will put their trust in You, for You, Lord, have not forsaken those who seek You. The Lord was pleased, for the sake of His righteousness, to make the Torah great and glorious.

<column-break/>

O Lord, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth.
Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the Lord.

And now, I pray, let the power of the Lord be great, as You have spoken, saying: Remember Your mercies, O Lord, and Your kindnesses, for they have been from of old.

<term>Kaddish</term> <gloss>Sanctification prayer</gloss>
Exalted and hallowed be His great name in the world which He created according to His will. May He establish His kingdom and cause His salvation to sprout and bring near the <insert>variant: the end of</insert> His Messiah. In your lifetime and in your days, and in the lifetime of the whole House of Israel, speedily and in a near time, and say, Amen. May His great name be blessed forever and to all eternity. Blessed and praised, glorified and exalted, extolled and honored, adored and lauded be the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, above <note>from time to time and above all</note> all the blessings and hymns, praises and consolations that are uttered in the world, and say, Amen. Receive, receive with mercy and favor our prayer. May the prayers and supplications of the whole House of Israel be accepted before their Father who is in heaven, and say, Amen. May the name of the Lord be blessed from this time forth and forever.

May there be abundant peace from heaven, and life for us and for all Israel, and say, Amen. My help is from the Lord, the Maker of heaven and earth. He who makes peace in His high places, may He make peace for us and for all Israel, and say, Amen.

### Chapter 3
### Examination of Intentions <note>original: "Bhava-pariksha"</note>

Even when an advance is made, women who are steady and bold must be tested. Because their true feelings are not easily revealed, a specific method of approach is required. Therefore, the examination of intentions is now discussed:

A man making an advance should observe the behavior of the woman; through that observation, her internal state is examined. (1)

Just as one approaches a young maiden, he should observe her behavior, meaning her physical gestures and movements. Indeed, by examining these, her true intention is tested. (1)

He explains how she is to be won over:

If she does not reveal the secret matter, he should win her over by using a female messenger <note>original: "dutya"</note>. (2)

Does not reveal the secret matter means she does not openly show her sexual feelings. Because of her boldness or reserve, he should win her over through a female messenger. (2)

If she rejects an advance but continues to associate with the man, he should know that her mind is divided into two. He should win her over gradually. (3)

Rejecting an advance means she refuses the proposal made by the hero <note>original: "nayaka"</note>. If, after some days have passed, she is found associating with him again, meaning she seeks his company, he should understand her to be of a divided mind. This is because her state must be tested; she feels, "I do not know what I should do." He should win her over step by step and not abandon her suddenly. (3)

He mentions a specific detail here:

If she rejects the advance but appears again particularly well-adorned, then likewise...

reluctance often caused him to avoid displaying his skill in formal disputation. In his manner of life he was not simple, but while practicing extreme temperance, he made use of expensive comforts. He habitually wore white garments and bathed twice a day in the public baths. Once, when someone asked him why he, being a bishop, bathed twice a day, he replied: Because I cannot manage a third. On another occasion, while observing Bishop Sergius at that time, he was asked by one of the associates of Arsacius why he wore clothing unsuited to a bishop, and where it was written that a priest should dress in white. He said: You tell me first where it is written that a bishop should wear black garments. When the questioner was at a loss, Sisinnius followed up his counter-question: Indeed, you would not be able to show that a priest must be clothed in black. But Solomon exhorted me, saying, let your garments be white. And the Savior in the Gospels appears using white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah wearing white to the apostles. Having readily said these and many other things, he was greatly admired by those present. When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia Minor, was taking away a church from the <term>Novatians</term> while visiting Constantinople, Sisinnius went to him and urged him to return the church. But Leontius answered warmly and said to him: You <term>Novatians</term> ought not to have churches, since you do away with repentance and shut out the loving-kindness of God. When Leontius had said these and many other such harsh things against the <term>Novatians</term>, Sisinnius said: Truly, no one has ever repented as much as I have. When the other asked again, how have you repented? Sisinnius answered: Because I have seen you. Once when John the bishop was making some accusation against him and saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said: For indeed it does not have two. When John became angry and said, you see that you alone are a bishop by your own reckoning, Sisinnius said: I do not say that, but that I am not a bishop only in your eyes, as I am in the ears of the people. John, becoming indignant at what was said, said: But I shall stop you from preaching, for you are a heretic. To this Sisinnius wittily replied: Indeed, I would even give you a reward if you would relieve me of such great labor. John, softened by the reply, said: I will not stop your freedom of speech if speaking is such a burden to you. Such then was Sisinnius, ready with replies and full of grace. To write and record all his sayings would be a long task. Therefore, I have shown by these few examples what kind of man he was, having considered it proper to rule. I say this: that all know him for his learning, and because of this, all the successive bishops loved and honored him. Moreover, all the prominent members of the Senate cherished and admired him. Many books were written by him, in which he used a refined style and mixed in poetic expressions. He was admired more when speaking than when read. For there was such grace in his face, his voice, his bearing, his look, and in every movement of his body. He was loved for these things by all the religious sects, and especially by Bishop Atticus. Such then are the matters concerning Sisinnius.

The table of life annuities therefore makes known what the person must pay annually to the fund to secure this capital after their death.

Maritime insurance, insurance against fire and storms, and generally all establishments of this kind, are calculated by the same principles. A merchant has ships at sea; they wish to insure their value and that of their cargo against the dangers they may run. For this, they give a sum to a company, which guarantees the estimated value of their cargoes and ships. Isaac was refined, the "severed male" who pitied his portion; Heaven forbid that he should be angry, for he was not like his portion. And behold, Isaac — is he not <term>Chesed</term>? He bowed, and it is established that all of them are <term>Din</term>. Is he not <term>Rachamim</term>? He bowed, and <term>Rachamim</term> is the King. Wisdom inherits <term>Chesed</term>, for <term>Chesed</term> bows, and Isaac as <term>Din</term> is from <term>Chesed</term>. Isaac bowed in <term>Rachamim</term>; is he not harsh <term>Din</term>? And so it was above, this from that, and it emerged from this until that, until all was known as one. And they all depend on one another, and for all to be found as one, the Heavens are needed forever and ever. **Rabbi Eleazar** recognized that there are no markings for her when we see her as one, and one is desired in both of them to complete everything, such as Jacob, and this is what is written:
> passing through from end to end <margin>Exodus 26:28</margin>

Everything is proven, for if you only read from our side and from our side, everything is known as one power; everything rises in one balance, it does not change and will not be changed, as it is written:
> I am the Lord, I change not <margin>Malachi 3:6</margin>

**Rabbi Yehuda** [said]: all the hidden things shine from one another and depend on one another, and their foundations are one, everything, not to be separated. And whoever separates them by his power is separated from the life of the worlds. **Rabbi Isaac** [said]: it is written:
> And I will give children to be their princes, and babes shall rule over them <margin>Isaiah 3:4</margin>

This is what is written: "impudent faces," "Cherubim," and this. And it is written: "He who sits upon the Cherubim," and it is written: "And He rode upon a Cherub and did fly." "He who sits upon the Cherubim" is when He begins to dwell in support; it is written "He who sits upon the Cherubim" (this is when He is found in perfection). Woe to the world when one Cherub turns its face away, for behold it is written:

This is when there was peace in the world. **Rabbi Isaac** [said]: we have learned, "the nakedness of a daughter-in-law and the youth of your father-in-law you shall not uncover." Woe to him who uncovers their nakedness. In this manner it is written of Jacob: "passing through from end to end." And thus the portion of Israel with the Holy One, blessed be He, is found in their adornments, in the manner of that which is above, as it is written:

Come and see, **Rabbi Isaac** [said]: in former days, it was that when one said to his fellow, "Show me one vessel and take money for it." And as in the Book of Concealment it is proven: woe above, woe below, and all of them rise in one balance. A parable of a man who lived in the fields and did not know of the dwellers of the city. He sowed wheat and ate wheat in its raw form. One day he entered the city, and they brought before him a good bread. He said: "What is this man eating?" They said: "It is bread to eat." He tasted them and said: "And what are these made of?" They said: "Wheat." Later they brought before him the royal pastries kneaded with honey and oil. For one who has a portion in the holy people must show [himself] greater than all in faith, to receive the guests, to rejoice in this world and in the world to come. Now that they invite him, and all the righteous, and King <term>David</term>, and they are not given their portion, this is the hardest of all, and it is called:

And they all go up and say: <term>Isaac</term> says:

<term>Jacob</term> says:

And all the rest of the righteous say:

King <term>David</term> says—and the laws of oppression [apply]—as it is written: "And it was like the lead of the seas," and "The Lord shall wave," regarding all. And when does he strike? > **Then shall you delight yourself in the Lord, etc.** <note>Isaiah 58:14</note>

And <term>Isaac</term> calls upon him:

Rabbi Shimon said: This King <term>David</term> says it, because all the weapons of the King and the battles of the King were entrusted into the hands of <term>David</term>. These matters are commonly proposed by theologians who instruct the internal tribunal of the soul.

III. First, it appears that a possessor in good faith (for a possessor in bad faith is held liable beyond the value of the property due to their own action) is not held to any restitution if the item has perished, because neither the item remains with them, nor any gain from the item.

<margin>Medina on contracts, q. 10. Zeffi, Book II, ch. 14. Navarro, ch. 17, no. 7.</margin>
IV. Second, a possessor in good faith is held to restore even the existing fruits of the item; I say the fruits of the item, for the fruits of one's own labor, even if they would not have come about without the item, are not owed to the owner of the item. The cause of this obligation arises from ownership, for he who is the owner of the item is naturally also the owner of the fruits of the item.

V. Third, a possessor in good faith is held to the restitution of both the item and the consumed fruits, provided that they would have consumed just as much in any other way; for in this, they are considered enriched. Thus, Gaius Caesar Caligula is praised at the beginning of his reign for having added the fruits of the intervening time to those to whom he restored their kingdoms.

<margin>Suetonius, ch. 16.</margin>
VI. Fourth, they are not held to the fruits which they neglected to collect, because they possess neither the item nor anything that succeeds in the place of the item.

VII. Fifth, if such a possessor gives away an item donated to them to another, they are not held liable unless they would have donated just as much even without this item, for then it would be a gain to have spared their own property.

<margin>Law: "Quivas," § last, Digest, on theft.</margin>
VIII. Sixth, if they sell an item they bought, they are not held liable unless perhaps they sold it for more; but if they sell an item that was donated to them, they are held to restore the price, unless perhaps they squandered the price, which they would not otherwise have squandered.

<margin>Law: "Si et rem," Digest, on the petition of inheritance.</margin>
IX. Seventh, an item belonging to another, bought in good faith, must be restored, and the price expended cannot be reclaimed. To this rule, it seems to me, an exception must be added: unless the owner could not have recovered possession of their property without some expense, for instance, if the item was in the hands of pirates. Then, the amount the owner would have gladly spent may be deducted. For the very possession of the fact, especially when recovery is difficult, is something of value, and in this, the owner is considered to have become enriched after the loss of the item. And therefore, although the purchase of one's own item is not valid under ordinary law, the jurist Paulus says that it is valid if it was agreed from the beginning that the possession which is with another is to be bought. Nor do I require here that the item be bought with the intention that it be restored to the owner, in which case some say that an action for the management of affairs arises.

<margin>Law: "Sed et si lege," Digest, on the same. Law: "Si eum servum," Digest, on loaned items. Law: "Mater tua," Law: "Si mancipia," Digest, on the vindication of property. Law: "Sucr.," Digest, on contracts of sale. Law: 1, Digest, on evictions. Law: "Si laborav," § "Si navis," Digest, on the Rhodian Law. Concerning those who buy from plunder, see Aegidius Regius, disp. 35, dub. 7, no. 126. Hostensis, title on the Law of War. Law: "Si in emtione," § "rei," Digest, on contracts of sale.</margin>

text:
<meta>The text contains commentaries on Chapter 48 and the beginning of Chapter 49 of the Tao Te Ching.</meta>

<margin>Su's Commentary</margin> Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> and devote themselves to learning find that what they hear and see increases daily, yet they have nothing to unify it; this inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much and select what is good to follow; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day you know the <term>Tao</term>, you look back at all that was false; everything done was nothing but delusion. To remove delusion and return to nature is what is called "decreasing." Confucius said to Zigong: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it with one principle." Forgetting the mind to purely return to nature is what is called decreasing; yet as long as delusions remain, one must reach the point of forgetting the mind itself to purely return to nature. Only when nothing remains do you leave behind "doing" and yet do not fail at "non-doing." Everyone has the desire to take hold of the world and finish its affairs; thus they create tasks and seek results. When this intention is seen outwardly, things resist it; therefore it is difficult and cannot be achieved. The Sage practices non-doing, so his mind is without affairs. When this is seen outwardly, things are at peace with him. Although he does not "take" the world's affairs to act upon them, the affairs of the world find order and peace therein.

<margin>Lü's Commentary</margin> Practicing learning is for those who have not yet heard the <term>Tao</term>. Those who have not heard the <term>Tao</term> and seek it cannot avoid being broad, hence it is called "daily increase." Practicing the <term>Tao</term> is for those who have already heard the <term>Tao</term>. Those who have heard the <term>Tao</term> and practice it cannot avoid simply practicing non-doing, hence it is called "daily decrease." To decrease and further decrease is for those who have not yet escaped "doing." When even the one who decreases is himself decreased, only then does one arrive at non-doing. Non-doing means being still and unmoving. Doing nothing left undone means being stimulated and thereby penetrating all the causes under heaven. Arriving at non-doing through non-doing is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called the Divine. The direction of the Divine is what is called the <term>Tao</term>. As for the Supreme Divine, who can partake in this? From this perspective, taking the world is always done through non-doing. By the time one resorts to "doing," it is clear they are insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai's Commentary</margin> Only after there is nothing one does not know can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires daily increase. Only after there is nothing one does not do can one speak of the <term>Tao</term>; therefore, the <term>Tao</term> desires daily decrease. However, that which increases can be pursued through progress, while that which decreases is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly shed everything and reach the realm of non-doing. Thus they can leave nothing undone, and their applications are inexhaustible, operating in the world with ample ease.

While he was explaining these matters concerning her, Lyciscus took the maiden and fled to Sparta. When the Messenians fell into despair upon learning that Lyciscus had fled, Aristodemus, a man of the Aepytid race and more distinguished than Lyciscus both in general reputation and in matters of war, offered his own daughter to be sacrificed voluntarily. But human destiny often conceals its purpose behind such eagerness, as silt in a river covers a pebble. Even then, when Aristodemus was striving to save the Messenians, destiny brought the following obstacle. A man of the Messenians (whose name they do not mention) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus. At that time, he was already about to take her as his wife. Secondly, when he saw this was not succeeding, he turned to a shameless argument, claiming he had slept with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. Finally, he provoked Aristodemus to such an extent that, driven mad by rage, he killed his daughter. Afterwards, he cut her open and demonstrated that she was not with child. Epebolus, being present, then ordered that someone else must offer a daughter; for the death of Aristodemus's daughter had gained them nothing, since the father had murdered her, rather than sacrificing her to the gods the Pythian oracle had commanded. When the seer spoke thus, the multitude of Messenians rushed forward to kill the suitor of the girl, as he had brought a senseless pollution upon Aristodemus and made their hope of salvation uncertain. This man, however, was a very close friend to Euphaes. Euphaes persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had been fulfilled by the girl's death, and that what Aristodemus had done was sufficient for them. The kings, following this advice, dissolved the assembly; and from there they turned to sacrifices and a festival of the gods. You will find this in the creation of the first man, in his judgment, and in his expulsion, and in all those matters. You will find that they all came about through the Attribute of Justice and the Attribute of Mercy, and everything was in perfect completion through mercy and justice, all according to what is fitting in true judgment. And according to this principle, the Torah said: The Rock, His work is perfect. And the explanation of the verse is this: The Rock who decrees judgment with strength does not act with cruelty; He does not decree judgment except that His work is perfect, meaning that the judgment He decreed previously was deliberated upon by the two attributes: Lovingkindness and Justice. And this is His work is perfect. For the term <term>Tamim</term> [perfect] is the secret of two things, and it is as if it said <term>Teumim</term> [twins], except that in the language of honor it speaks of two things on high using the term <term>Tamim</term>, and below it uses the term <term>Teumim</term>. And so it says: and they shall be doubled [<term>Teumim</term>] from below together they shall be whole [<term>Tamim</term>] at its top. Below they are twins, above they are perfect, because below they appear as two things, a thing and its opposite, like a supporter and an accuser; but above, everything is one intention. Whether it is the supporter or the accuser, they both have one intention, and there is no hatred or love there, and there is no favoritism there, but rather true judgment. Therefore it said, His work is perfect: through justice and mercy He deliberated and decreed the judgment, and this is the secret of true judgment. And as for what it said, for all His ways are justice, the explanation is that everything is before the eye of every observer, as it says: for all His ways are justice. And you already know that Justice is included in Judgment and Mercy, for Justice corresponds to Jacob, who is the Middle Pillar that mediates between the two tents which are Abraham and Isaac. Abraham corresponds to Lovingkindness, Isaac corresponds to Judgment, and Jacob decides between them: a perfect man, dwelling in tents. And Justice corresponds to Jacob, drawing from Lovingkindness from the side of Abraham and from Judgment from the side of Isaac. And so it says: Justice and righteousness in Jacob You have made. And the prophet said: Correct me, O <term>YHVH</term>, but with justice, not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing. And the explanation of the verse Correct me, O <term>YHVH</term>, but with justice: what it said <term>Ach</term> [but] is a division, as if to say, with half the attribute of Justice, which is Lovingkindness, for Justice is half Judgment and half Lovingkindness. Therefore it said, but with justice, and said afterward, not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing, and it revealed the secret to diminish the half of Justice that comes from the side of anger. Therefore, Justice is dependent on Jacob, who is the father among the tribes; he knew the great pain of children when the Holy One, Blessed be He, decrees upon them, so that he would seek mercy and righteousness for them. That is to say, when Justice is exalted, Judgment rests and turns to the attribute of <term>El</term>, which is the secret of what is said: And the holy God is sanctified in righteousness. Generally, when <term>YHVH</term> of Hosts is exalted in justice, the attribute of <term>El</term> comes, which is above, and performs righteousness and sweetens the Justice. And this is the secret of what they said: and Justice is included in Lovingkindness and Judgment, and it says: Justice and righteousness in Jacob You have made. **And he answered.** "These are the four winds." This is like "to the seven winds." Similarly, "and he came Jerusalem" is like "to Jerusalem." Another interpretation: like "a black son" is like "to a black son," and similar cases. It refers to the division of the four chariots and their going out to the seven winds of the heavens. It means giving permission to the seven kingdoms to rule in the seven winds, each one in its time. This refers to the whole world, which is a term for strength. "From standing before the Lord of all the earth." This refers to the mission from God who gave them power over this. Like "the sons of God came to stand before the Lord." <margin>Job 2</margin> **The one with.** The black ones. And it mentions the black ones because the time of the Babylonian kingdom had already passed. And the kingdom of Media and Persia would be first toward the north country, for they were there to destroy it, and afterwards they ruled over all the kingdoms of the earth. And the white ones, which is the kingdom of Greece, went out after them once the kingdom was established. For Alexander the Macedonian, the first king of Greece, killed Darius in Babylon and took the kingship from him and reigned, and after him his successors ruled throughout the whole world. **And the dappled ones went out to the south country.** This refers to the holy portion because Rome is <term>shinunit</term>, and Augustus Caesar, who ruled over Rome, began to fight against the kingdom of Greece. At the start of his wars, he went out to the land of Egypt, which is southern. At that time, the sons of Greece were ruling in all the lands. And Augustus Caesar prevailed over them, transferred the kingship from the sons of Greece, and returned it to the Romans. **And the strong ones.** They are a hint to the kingdom of Ishmael who strengthened themselves of their own accord to seek kingship, to have a place for their spirit. This is what is meant by "and they sought to go, to walk about through the earth." **And he said.** Meaning, he gave them permission to walk about and conquer lands. **And he cried out.** Meaning, he called to me with a loud voice and said to me, **"See, those going out to the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country."** Meaning the portion of the black ones who went out to Babylon to destroy it.

Certain superstitious men and sons of this age, wanting to heap errors upon errors, attempt to defend themselves beyond the understanding and intention of <term>Scotus</term> and the canonists with these arguments. They claim that natural things possess certain occult virtues, the reason for which cannot be assigned by man, just as the magnet attracts iron. There are many other such things that <term>Augustine</term> enumerates in the twenty-first book of *The City of God*. Therefore, they argue, it should be permitted to seek ways for health where charms and natural medicines fail; it would not be illicit, provided the means appear trivial, if one were to seek to procure health for oneself or another through images that are not <term>necromantic</term> or <term>astrological</term>, or through rings and the like. Furthermore, they argue: just as natural bodies are subject to celestial bodies, so also artificial bodies, such as images, obtain certain occult virtues, hoping to derive them from the influence of celestial bodies; therefore, artificial bodies, such as images, also obtain some occult virtues from celestial bodies to cause certain effects, and thus it is not illicit to use them and others of this kind. Furthermore, demons can transmute bodies in many ways, as <term>Augustine</term> says in the third book of *On the Trinity*, and it is evident in those who are bewitched; therefore, it is lawful to use even their power to remove those afflictions. 

But in truth, the sayings of all the holy doctors are to the contrary, and this has been made clear here and there in the preceding text. Wherefore, in response to the first point, it is said that if natural things are applied simply to produce certain effects for which they are thought to have a natural virtue, it is not illicit. If, however, they attach characters or any other unknown and vain observations that clearly do not have such efficacy by nature, it will be superstitious and illicit, as <term>Thomas</term> treats in the second part of the second book, question 96, article 2, at the end of the question.

<summary>This page addresses arguments made by superstitious individuals who seek to justify the use of occult images and charms for healing by appealing to natural virtues and celestial influences, and provides a theological rebuttal based on the teachings of Thomas Aquinas.</summary>
<keywords>superstition, occult virtues, natural medicine, celestial bodies, necromancy, astrology, demons, Thomas Aquinas, Saint Augustine</keywords>

<margin>By the flow of water itself in the middle they use a heart with a tongue for Egypt.</margin>
The divine water-jar, or a vessel gushing forth water for heaven and earth, is depicted by likening the water-jar to a heart that has a tongue. It is likened to a heart because among them this is the ruling part of the body, just as the Nile is established as the ruler of Egypt. It is likened to a tongue because the tongue always exists in moisture and they call it the parent of what is good. They use water-jars that are neither more nor less [than two], because the operation of the rising of the Nile consists of two parts according to them. They designate one for the land of Egypt, since Egypt is by itself generative of water. The other they designate for the ocean, for from it water arrives in Egypt at the time of the rising. They attribute the abundance to the rains which occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia during the season of the rising of the Nile. That Egypt generates the water is possible to learn from this: in the rest of the climate of the world, the floods of the rivers are completed in the winter.

<summary>This page explains the hieroglyphic symbolism of the water-jar, heart, and tongue as representations of Egypt and the Nile's flooding. It discusses the dual origins of the river's rise from both the Egyptian soil and the southern rains of Ethiopia.</summary>
<keywords>Nile, Egypt, water-jar, heart, tongue, Ethiopia, flooding, hieroglyphics</keywords>

Xiangling smiled, "No wonder when I used to peek at one or two poems in old books, some were perfectly matched and others were not. I also heard people say, 'the first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Looking at the poems of the ancients, some followed this and others were wrong on the second, fourth, and sixth. I was confused every day. Now hearing you speak, it turns out these rules do not matter as long as the phrasing is novel and original." Daiyu said, "That is exactly the point. Phrasing is a secondary matter; the most important thing is the intent. If the intent and interest are genuine, the poem will be good even without polishing the phrasing. This is called 'not letting the words harm the intent.'"

Xiangling said, "I only love Lu Fangweng's 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, keeping the fragrance long; the old inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It is so vivid and interesting!" Daiyu said, "Because you do not understand poetry, you love what is shallow and accessible. Once you enter that pattern, you will never be able to break out of it. Listen to me: if you truly want to learn, I have the <term>Complete Works of Wang Mojie</term>. Take his one hundred five-character regulated poems and ponder them until you know them thoroughly. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's seven-character regulated poems, followed by one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three as a foundation in your belly, then look at the works of Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, Bao, and others. Being as clever and sharp as you are, in less than a year’s work, you need not worry about not becoming a master poet!" Hearing this, Xiangling smiled, "If so, dear Miss, please bring those books out for me. I will take them back and it will be good to recite a few poems at night." Regarding this, monks, there are those recluses and brahmins who hold this doctrine and this view: "Whatever a person experiences, whether pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling, all of it is caused by the creation of a supreme deity." I go to them and say: "Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold this doctrine and this view: 'Whatever a person experiences, whether pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling, all of it is caused by the creation of a supreme deity'?"

When I ask them this, if they acknowledge it, saying, "Yes." <margin>D. and T. manuscripts read <term>âmo</term>.</margin>

I say to them: "Then, venerable sirs, people will be killers of living beings because of the creation of a supreme deity... and so on... they will be of wrong view because of the creation of a supreme deity. Monks, for those who fall back on the creation of a supreme deity as the essential truth, there is no desire, no effort, no 'this should be done' or 'this should not be done.' Thus, when what should and should not be done is not found to be true or certain, for those who live with muddled mindfulness and without protection, there is no legitimate, righteous claim to being a recluse."

Monks, this is my second righteous rebuttal to those recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view.

<summary>The Buddha critiques the views that human experience and moral actions are determined solely by past karma or by the will of a supreme deity. He argues that such fatalistic views negate the necessity of human effort and moral responsibility.</summary>

# We have set the distance

from midday because the adjustment for births is easier with it than working with horizons; and the hours of the longest day for the latitude of Jerusalem are fourteen hours and some, so the calculation of the Jews using <term>temporal hours</term> is not correct unless the conjunction for the beginning of <term>Tishrei</term> happens to coincide with the autumnal equinox. It never actually coincides with it, but rather precedes or follows it by a significant amount, as we have demonstrated previously. Once we have extracted the time of the conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table we analyzed according to their view, we progress from that to the knowledge of the first day of the year and the determination of its state regarding deficiency, regularity, or completeness. We already possess the knowledge of whether the year is common or leap. We then seek in the table of limits a period of weekdays whose two boundaries encompass the time in which the conjunction occurred for us—on the side of the leap years if it is a leap year, and on the side of the common years if it is common. When we find it, we find alongside it the first day of the week for the year and its state. When we know the beginning of the year and its state, and combine that state with its status as common or leap, we know from that the passing of the beginning of the following year.
